title: Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding
what_it_is: Water is a polar molecule. Its uneven charge distribution allows water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with each other and with other polar or charged substances.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting a property of water to the molecular reason behind it and then to the biological consequence.
answer_move: Use a three-step chain: water is polar -> hydrogen bonds form -> this causes the biological property or effect.
common_point_loss: Naming a water property without explaining how polarity or hydrogen bonding produces it.

title: Elements of Life
what_it_is: Living systems are built mostly from a small set of elements, especially carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking an element to the molecule or structure it supports, such as phosphorus in nucleic acids and phospholipids or nitrogen in amino acids and nucleotides.
answer_move: Do not just list elements. Connect the element to a biological molecule and the molecule to its function.
common_point_loss: Reciting CHNOPS without explaining what those elements let cells build or do.

title: Introduction to Macromolecules
what_it_is: Biological macromolecules are large molecules built from smaller subunits. Dehydration synthesis builds polymers by removing water, and hydrolysis breaks polymers by adding water.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying whether a system is building or breaking a polymer and by connecting the reaction to water use or release and bond formation or cleavage.
answer_move: Ask: is the cell building a larger molecule or breaking one apart? Then name dehydration synthesis or hydrolysis and state what happens to water.
common_point_loss: Mixing up dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis, especially the direction of water movement.

title: Carbohydrates
what_it_is: Carbohydrates include monosaccharides and polysaccharides. They can provide readily usable energy, store energy, or contribute to structural support depending on their bonds and organization.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting carbohydrate structure to function, such as glucose availability for energy, starch or glycogen for storage, or cellulose for plant cell wall support.
answer_move: Name the carbohydrate type, identify the structural feature, and connect it to energy storage, energy use, or support.
common_point_loss: Saying carbohydrates are only for energy and missing structural roles such as cellulose.

title: Lipids
what_it_is: Lipids are generally nonpolar or hydrophobic molecules. Important examples include fats, phospholipids, and steroids, each with structures that support different cell functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting nonpolar or amphipathic structure to function. For example, phospholipid structure explains membrane formation, while fats support long-term energy storage.
answer_move: Start with polarity: hydrophobic or amphipathic? Then connect that property to membrane behavior, storage, insulation, or signaling.
common_point_loss: Treating all lipids as the same instead of distinguishing fats, phospholipids, and steroids by structure and function.

title: Nucleic Acids
what_it_is: Nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides. Their nucleotide sequences store and transmit biological information.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting nucleotide structure and sequence to information storage, directionality, complementary base pairing, or differences between DNA and RNA.
answer_move: When asked about DNA or RNA, connect structure to information: sequence stores instructions, base pairing supports copying, and strand direction affects synthesis.
common_point_loss: Describing nucleic acids only as genetic material without explaining how sequence, base pairing, or strand structure supports the function.

title: Proteins
what_it_is: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. A protein's amino acid sequence influences its folding, shape, and function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracing the structure-function chain: amino acid sequence affects interactions, interactions affect folding and shape, and shape affects protein function.
answer_move: Use the chain: sequence -> folding/shape -> function. If a mutation or environmental change appears, explain how it could alter that chain.
common_point_loss: Saying a protein is denatured or changed without connecting the structural change to a functional consequence.

title: Cell Structure and Function
what_it_is: Cells contain specialized structures whose shapes and locations support specific biological functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting a cell structure to the process it supports and explaining why that structure helps the process happen.
answer_move: Name the structure, name the function, then explain the feature that makes the function possible.
common_point_loss: Listing organelles without connecting structure to function.

title: Cell Size
what_it_is: Cell size is constrained by surface area-to-volume ratio and the need to exchange materials efficiently.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting size changes to surface area, volume, exchange rate, and limits on cellular function.
answer_move: Compare surface area and volume as size changes, then state the effect on exchange efficiency.
common_point_loss: Saying small cells are efficient without explaining the surface area-to-volume relationship.

title: Plasma Membrane
what_it_is: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that separates internal and external environments.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting phospholipid amphipathic structure and membrane proteins to selective movement or communication.
answer_move: Start with bilayer structure, then identify the protein or lipid feature responsible for the observed function.
common_point_loss: Calling the membrane a barrier without explaining selective permeability.

title: Membrane Permeability
what_it_is: Membrane permeability depends on molecule size, polarity, charge, and whether transport proteins are available.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining movement based on molecular properties and membrane composition.
answer_move: Ask whether the molecule is small/nonpolar, polar, charged, or large, then decide if a protein is needed.
common_point_loss: Saying molecules cross because the cell needs them instead of because their properties allow it.

title: Membrane Transport
what_it_is: Membrane transport includes passive movement down gradients and active movement requiring energy to move against gradients.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the gradient, direction of movement, energy requirement, and protein involvement.
answer_move: State high-to-low or low-to-high relative to the gradient, then name passive or active transport.
common_point_loss: Ignoring gradient direction or claiming all protein transport requires ATP.

title: Facilitated Diffusion
what_it_is: Facilitated diffusion uses membrane proteins to move substances down their concentration gradients without direct energy input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining that a specific channel or carrier allows movement down the gradient.
answer_move: Name the transport protein type and make clear the movement is passive and down gradient.
common_point_loss: Calling facilitated diffusion active transport because a protein is involved.

title: Tonicity and Osmoregulation
what_it_is: Tonicity describes how surrounding solute concentration affects water movement across membranes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the relative solute concentrations, predicting water movement, and explaining the effect on the cell.
answer_move: Compare solute inside and outside, then move water toward the higher solute concentration.
common_point_loss: Moving solute instead of water when answering an osmosis question.

title: Mechanisms of Transport
what_it_is: Cells use channels, carriers, pumps, endocytosis, and exocytosis to move materials across membranes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the mechanism that fits the substance and explaining why that mechanism is needed.
answer_move: Match molecule size and gradient direction to channel, carrier, pump, endocytosis, or exocytosis.
common_point_loss: Naming a mechanism without justifying why the cell would use it for that material.

title: Cell Compartmentalization
what_it_is: Compartmentalization separates cellular processes into membrane-bound spaces with distinct conditions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking a compartment to the process it supports and the advantage of separation.
answer_move: Identify the compartment, the process inside it, and the benefit of separating that process.
common_point_loss: Saying organelles are specialized without explaining the advantage of compartment boundaries.

title: Origins of Cell Compartmentalization
what_it_is: Endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts from ancestral prokaryotes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from once free-living prokaryotic cells by endosymbiosis, supporting it with evidence such as their double membranes, and contrasting how prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells compartmentalize.
answer_move: State the endosymbiotic origin, then compare: prokaryotes have specialized internal regions without membrane-bound organelles, while eukaryotes partition the cell with internal membranes.
common_point_loss: Naming mitochondria and chloroplasts without saying they came from free-living prokaryotes, or claiming prokaryotes have no internal organization at all.

title: Enzymes
what_it_is: Enzymes are biological catalysts whose active sites help lower activation energy for specific reactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting active-site shape, substrate specificity, and activation energy to reaction outcomes.
answer_move: Describe how enzyme structure affects substrate binding and reaction rate.
common_point_loss: Saying enzymes add energy to reactions instead of lowering activation energy.

title: Environmental Impacts on Enzyme Function
what_it_is: Temperature, pH, salinity, and other conditions can alter enzyme shape and activity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking environmental change to protein structure, active-site fit, and reaction rate.
answer_move: Use data to identify the activity change, then explain it through enzyme shape or denaturation when appropriate.
common_point_loss: Only describing the graph trend without explaining the molecular cause.

title: Cellular Energy
what_it_is: Cells use energy coupling and ATP to drive processes that require energy input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining how ATP hydrolysis or coupled reactions make an unfavorable process possible.
answer_move: Identify the energy-requiring process and connect ATP or coupling to the work being done.
common_point_loss: Saying ATP is energy without explaining how phosphate transfer or coupling supports the process.

title: Photosynthesis
what_it_is: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars through linked light reactions and carbon fixation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking inputs, locations, products, and energy transformations across the two major stages.
answer_move: Separate light reactions from the Calvin cycle, then connect their products and dependencies.
common_point_loss: Mixing up where oxygen, ATP, NADPH, or sugar are produced.

title: Cellular Respiration
what_it_is: Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP through glycolysis, oxidation steps, and electron transport.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting molecule breakdown, electron carriers, proton gradients, oxygen, and ATP production.
answer_move: Track carbon, electrons, and ATP through the process instead of memorizing a list of stages.
common_point_loss: Saying oxygen makes ATP directly instead of explaining its role as final electron acceptor.

title: Cell Communication
what_it_is: Cell communication uses signals, receptors, and responses to coordinate activity across cells.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting signal reception to a cellular response and explaining how specificity is achieved.
answer_move: Identify the signal, receptor, target cell, and response in order.
common_point_loss: Saying a signal causes a response without explaining receptor specificity.

title: Introduction to Signal Transduction
what_it_is: Signal transduction converts an external or internal signal into intracellular molecular changes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining the sequence reception -> transduction -> response.
answer_move: Use the three-stage chain and place each molecule or event in the correct stage.
common_point_loss: Skipping from signal to response without describing intracellular transduction.

title: Signal Transduction Pathways
what_it_is: Signal transduction pathways often use cascades, phosphorylation, second messengers, and amplification.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracing pathway order and explaining how changes to one component affect downstream response.
answer_move: Follow the pathway arrow by arrow and state whether each step activates, inhibits, or amplifies the next.
common_point_loss: Describing every component as simply on or off without linking upstream changes to downstream effects.

title: Feedback
what_it_is: Feedback loops regulate biological systems by using outputs to influence earlier steps.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the variable, stimulus, response, and whether the loop reduces or amplifies the original change.
answer_move: Ask whether the response reverses the change or strengthens it, then name negative or positive feedback.
common_point_loss: Calling every control system negative feedback without explaining the direction of the response.

title: Cell Cycle
what_it_is: The cell cycle coordinates growth, DNA replication, and division through ordered phases.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by placing events in the correct phase and explaining why ordering matters for accurate division.
answer_move: Name the phase and the key event: growth, DNA replication, chromosome separation, or cytokinesis.
common_point_loss: Mixing up DNA replication with chromosome separation.

title: Regulation of Cell Cycle
what_it_is: Cell cycle checkpoints and regulatory proteins help prevent division when DNA or cell conditions are not ready.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining how checkpoint failure or regulatory disruption changes cell division outcomes.
answer_move: Identify the checkpoint or regulator, then state what error it normally prevents.
common_point_loss: Saying cells divide too fast without explaining the failed control mechanism.

title: Meiosis
what_it_is: Meiosis produces haploid gametes through two divisions after one round of DNA replication.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracking homologous chromosomes, sister chromatids, ploidy, and gamete outcomes across meiosis I and II.
answer_move: Separate meiosis I from meiosis II: homologs separate first, sister chromatids separate second.
common_point_loss: Confusing meiosis with mitosis or losing track of chromosome number changes.

title: Meiosis and Genetic Diversity
what_it_is: Crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation among gametes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting a meiotic event to new allele combinations in gametes or offspring.
answer_move: Name crossing over or independent assortment and explain the specific source of variation.
common_point_loss: Saying meiosis creates diversity without identifying the mechanism.

title: Mendelian Genetics
what_it_is: Mendelian genetics predicts inheritance patterns for traits controlled by alleles that segregate and assort.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by assigning genotypes, setting up crosses, and interpreting probabilities or phenotypic ratios.
answer_move: Define alleles and parental genotypes before building the Punnett square or probability setup.
common_point_loss: Reporting ratios without connecting them to genotype and allele segregation.

title: Non-Mendelian Genetics
what_it_is: Non-Mendelian patterns include inheritance that does not follow simple dominant-recessive single-gene expectations.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the inheritance pattern from evidence and adjusting genotype-to-phenotype reasoning accordingly.
answer_move: Use the data pattern to choose the inheritance model before calculating outcomes.
common_point_loss: Forcing every trait into a simple dominant-recessive Punnett square.

title: Environmental Effects on Phenotype
what_it_is: Phenotype results from genotype interacting with environmental conditions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining how an environmental factor changes gene expression, development, or observable trait value.
answer_move: State genotype potential and then explain how the environment shifts the phenotype.
common_point_loss: Claiming the environment changes the DNA sequence when the prompt describes phenotype plasticity.

title: DNA and RNA Structure
what_it_is: DNA and RNA are nucleic acids with nucleotide sequences, sugar-phosphate backbones, and base-pairing rules.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting base sequence, complementarity, directionality, and DNA/RNA differences to biological function.
answer_move: Use structure-function language: base order stores information and base pairing enables accurate copying or expression.
common_point_loss: Saying DNA stores information without explaining sequence or base pairing.

title: DNA Replication
what_it_is: DNA replication copies genetic information using complementary base pairing and enzyme-coordinated strand synthesis.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining template strands, complementary nucleotides, directionality, and enzyme roles in accurate copying.
answer_move: Describe how each original strand guides a new complementary strand.
common_point_loss: Saying DNA duplicates without explaining templating or complementary base pairing.

title: Transcription and RNA Processing
what_it_is: Transcription produces RNA from a DNA template, and RNA processing modifies eukaryotic transcripts before translation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing template DNA, mRNA product, RNA polymerase, and processing steps such as splicing when relevant.
answer_move: Track information flow from DNA template to RNA sequence, then mention processing if the organism or prompt requires it.
common_point_loss: Confusing transcription with translation or treating introns as protein-coding sequences.

title: Translation
what_it_is: Translation uses ribosomes, mRNA codons, tRNA anticodons, and amino acids to build polypeptides.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting codon sequence to amino acid sequence and explaining the roles of ribosome and tRNA.
answer_move: Read mRNA codons in order and connect each codon to an amino acid carried by tRNA.
common_point_loss: Using the DNA template directly as the codon sequence without transcribing to mRNA.

title: Regulation of Gene Expression
what_it_is: Cells regulate gene expression by controlling when and how much gene product is made.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the control point and explaining how it changes mRNA or protein production.
answer_move: State whether regulation affects transcription, RNA processing, translation, or protein activity, then explain the output change.
common_point_loss: Saying a gene is turned on or off without identifying the regulatory mechanism or product effect.

title: Gene Expression and Cell Specialization
what_it_is: Different cell types can contain the same genome but express different genes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining that selective gene expression produces different proteins and therefore different cell functions.
answer_move: Connect gene expression pattern -> protein set -> specialized cell function.
common_point_loss: Claiming specialized cells have different DNA when the prompt concerns differential gene expression.

title: Mutations
what_it_is: Mutations are changes in genetic information that can alter RNA, protein sequence, protein function, or phenotype.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracing the effect of a mutation from DNA change to codon, amino acid, protein structure, and phenotype when appropriate.
answer_move: Follow the chain: DNA mutation -> RNA/codon change -> amino acid or regulation change -> functional effect.
common_point_loss: Stopping at mutation happened without explaining the downstream consequence.

title: Biotechnology
what_it_is: Biotechnology uses molecular tools to analyze, modify, or compare DNA and gene expression.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining what the tool measures or changes and how the result supports a biological claim.
answer_move: Identify the method's input, output, and interpretation before answering the claim.
common_point_loss: Naming a technique without explaining what the data show.

title: Introduction to Natural Selection
what_it_is: Natural selection occurs when heritable variation affects survival or reproduction in a particular environment.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting variation, heritability, differential fitness, and allele frequency change.
answer_move: Use the chain: variation exists -> some variants improve fitness -> those alleles become more common.
common_point_loss: Saying organisms adapt because they need to change.

title: Natural Selection
what_it_is: Natural selection changes population traits over generations because individuals with certain heritable traits leave more offspring.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining selection pressure, fitness differences, inheritance, and population-level change over time.
answer_move: Describe what is selected, why it affects reproductive success, and how the population changes.
common_point_loss: Describing individual organisms evolving during their lifetimes.

title: Artificial Selection
what_it_is: Artificial selection occurs when humans choose which traits are favored for breeding.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the human-selected trait and explaining how breeding changes trait or allele frequencies over generations.
answer_move: Name the selected trait, who selects it, and how reproduction changes the population.
common_point_loss: Calling artificial selection unnatural and missing the inheritance mechanism.

title: Population Genetics
what_it_is: Population genetics studies allele frequencies and how evolutionary forces change genetic composition.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by calculating or interpreting allele and genotype frequencies and linking changes to evolutionary mechanisms.
answer_move: Define the population and allele frequencies before deciding whether they changed.
common_point_loss: Confusing genotype frequency with allele frequency.

title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
what_it_is: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a null model for genotype frequencies when specific evolutionary conditions are met.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 and interpreting departures from expected frequencies.
answer_move: Identify p and q carefully, calculate genotype frequencies, then compare observed and expected values.
common_point_loss: Taking the square root of the wrong frequency or forgetting that 2pq is the heterozygote frequency.

title: Evidence of Evolution
what_it_is: Evidence for evolution includes fossils, molecular similarities, anatomical structures, biogeography, and observed population change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by naming specific evidence and explaining how it supports common ancestry or evolutionary change.
answer_move: Use claim-evidence-reasoning: state the evolutionary claim, cite the evidence, then explain the connection.
common_point_loss: Listing evidence types without tying them to the claim.

title: Common Ancestry
what_it_is: Common ancestry means groups share an ancestral lineage, often inferred from molecular or structural similarities.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using similarities and differences to infer relative relatedness or shared ancestry.
answer_move: Compare the evidence and state which organisms share a more recent common ancestor and why.
common_point_loss: Saying similar organisms are related without explaining what evidence supports recency of ancestry.

title: Continuing Evolution
what_it_is: Evolution continues when allele frequencies keep changing under mutation, selection, drift, or gene flow.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the evolutionary force and explaining how it changes allele frequencies over generations.
answer_move: Name the force causing change and connect it to allele-frequency shifts, not individual need.
common_point_loss: Describing short-term acclimation as evolution without heritable population change.

title: Phylogeny
what_it_is: Phylogenies represent hypotheses about evolutionary relationships among groups.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading nodes as common ancestors and using branching patterns, not tip order, to infer relationships.
answer_move: Find the most recent common ancestor on the tree before comparing relatedness.
common_point_loss: Comparing organisms by how close their labels appear at the tips instead of by shared nodes.

title: Speciation
what_it_is: Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated and diverge into separate species.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining the isolating barrier, reduced gene flow, divergence, and reproductive isolation.
answer_move: State what separates the populations and how separation leads to accumulated differences.
common_point_loss: Saying two species form because organisms choose different traits without explaining isolation and divergence.

title: Variations in Populations
what_it_is: Variation in populations comes from mutation, recombination, and other sources of genetic difference.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the source of variation and explaining how it creates differences selection or drift can act on.
answer_move: Connect the variation source to heritable differences among individuals.
common_point_loss: Saying the environment creates needed mutations for a trait.

title: Origins of Life on Earth
what_it_is: Origins-of-life questions address hypotheses about early conditions and the emergence of biological molecules and cells.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting early Earth conditions, chemical building blocks, and evidence to a plausible step in life's origin.
answer_move: State the hypothesis and the evidence or condition that supports it.
common_point_loss: Making a certainty claim where the question asks for evidence-based hypothesis reasoning.

title: Responses to the Environment
what_it_is: Organisms respond to environmental stimuli through behavioral, physiological, or developmental changes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking a stimulus to a response and explaining how the response affects survival, reproduction, or homeostasis.
answer_move: Identify stimulus, response, and biological advantage in the same answer.
common_point_loss: Describing behavior without explaining its effect on fitness or regulation.

title: Energy Flow Through Ecosystems
what_it_is: Energy flows through ecosystems from producers to consumers and is lost as heat at each transfer.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracing energy movement and explaining why available energy decreases at higher trophic levels.
answer_move: Follow energy from source to trophic level and account for loss at each transfer.
common_point_loss: Treating energy as recycled like matter.

title: Population Ecology
what_it_is: Population ecology studies population size, growth, carrying capacity, and factors that affect population change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting birth, death, immigration, emigration, resources, and carrying capacity to population trends.
answer_move: Read the graph or model first, then identify which factor changes population size.
common_point_loss: Calling every population increase exponential without checking limiting factors.

title: Effect of Density of Populations
what_it_is: Population density affects competition, disease spread, predation, and resource availability.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining how the effect changes as population density changes and what that does to growth or survival.
answer_move: Ask whether the factor becomes stronger when the population is more crowded.
common_point_loss: Mislabeling weather or natural disasters as density-dependent just because populations are affected.

title: Community Ecology
what_it_is: Community ecology studies interactions among species, including competition, predation, mutualism, parasitism, and succession.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the interaction type and explaining the effect on each species or on community composition.
answer_move: Name the interaction and state the effect on each participant using evidence from the prompt.
common_point_loss: Naming an interaction without explaining who benefits, is harmed, or is unaffected.

title: Biodiversity
what_it_is: Biodiversity includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting the type of biodiversity to stability, resilience, or response to environmental change.
answer_move: Specify genetic, species, or ecosystem diversity, then explain the consequence of more or less diversity.
common_point_loss: Saying biodiversity is good without explaining the mechanism or level of diversity.

title: Disruptions in Ecosystems
what_it_is: Disruptions such as habitat change, invasive species, climate shifts, and pollution can alter ecosystem structure and function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracing the disruption through direct and indirect effects on populations, interactions, and ecosystem processes.
answer_move: Identify the first affected component, then follow consequences through the system using evidence.
common_point_loss: Making a vague claim that the ecosystem is harmed without tracing a specific mechanism.

title: Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?
what_it_is: This topic introduces the move from average change over an interval to change at a single instant. A limit describes what average rates approach as the interval around the instant shrinks.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing whether a question asks about an interval or an instant and by connecting the instant case to limiting behavior.
answer_move: Ask: over an interval or at one point? If it is at one point, describe the instantaneous rate as the value approached by average rates over smaller intervals.
common_point_loss: Trying to compute an instantaneous rate as a direct quotient with zero change in x.

title: Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation
what_it_is: A limit describes the value a function approaches as x gets close to a chosen input. Limit notation names that approaching behavior precisely.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading and writing the approaching input, function, direction when specified, and value approached.
answer_move: Read the notation as: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L. Keep approaches separate from equals.
common_point_loss: Replacing the limit with f(a) automatically, or dropping the direction marker on a one-sided limit.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Graphs
what_it_is: A graph can show what y-value a function approaches as x moves toward a chosen input from the left, right, or both sides.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying left-hand and right-hand behavior and concluding whether the two-sided limit exists.
answer_move: Trace the graph toward the x-value from both sides before looking at the point on the graph.
common_point_loss: Using a filled or open point as the limit value without checking nearby graph behavior.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Tables
what_it_is: A table can suggest a limit by showing how function values behave for x-values close to a chosen input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using nearby table values from both sides and writing an estimate that matches the evidence.
answer_move: Look inward from both sides of the table, then state the trend and estimated limit.
common_point_loss: Choosing one table entry instead of describing the trend across nearby entries.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits
what_it_is: Limit properties let students combine simpler limits to determine limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and composite functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying a valid property, preserving expression structure, and showing setup that makes the final value follow.
answer_move: Break the expression into parts, determine component limits, then apply the matching property.
common_point_loss: Applying quotient or composition rules mechanically when the needed conditions are not met.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation
what_it_is: Some limit expressions hide their behavior until they are rewritten into an equivalent useful form.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing a valid rewrite, showing the transformed expression, and evaluating from the simplified form.
answer_move: When substitution is blocked, ask what equivalent form removes the obstacle.
common_point_loss: Stopping at 0/0, or canceling terms that are not common factors.

title: Selecting Procedures for Determining Limits
what_it_is: This topic is about choosing the method that fits the limit problem before carrying out the calculation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by classifying the problem form and selecting a procedure that matches it.
answer_move: Before solving, name the cue: direct substitution works, sides must be checked, factoring helps, or another strategy fits.
common_point_loss: Defaulting to a familiar technique without checking whether the problem calls for it.

title: Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem
what_it_is: The squeeze theorem finds a limit by trapping one function between two functions that approach the same value.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing bounds, showing both bounding limits match, and then stating the squeezed conclusion.
answer_move: Write the inequality first, find the outside limits, then conclude the middle limit.
common_point_loss: Naming the theorem without showing the bounding relationship and matching limits.

title: Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits
what_it_is: The same limit can be represented by notation, words, a graph, a table, or an equation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the same limiting behavior across representations and keeping the claim consistent.
answer_move: Convert each representation into: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L.
common_point_loss: Matching a table or graph to a function value instead of to approach behavior.

title: Exploring Types of Discontinuities
what_it_is: A discontinuity is a place where continuity fails. The type depends on whether the value, one-sided limits, or bounded behavior fails.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by classifying the discontinuity and connecting that classification to limit evidence.
answer_move: Check left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and f(c), then classify based on which part fails.
common_point_loss: Calling every gap removable or every discontinuity an asymptote without checking behavior.

title: Defining Continuity at a Point
what_it_is: A function is continuous at a point when f(c) exists, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(c).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking all three conditions and using them to justify whether the function is continuous.
answer_move: Use the checklist: value exists, limit exists, value equals limit, then state the conclusion.
common_point_loss: Saying a function is continuous because the graph looks connected without verifying conditions.

title: Confirming Continuity over an Interval
what_it_is: Continuity over an interval means the function is continuous at every point in that interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the interval, checking special points, and naming domain restrictions or endpoints that matter.
answer_move: Start with the function family and domain, then check special points inside the interval.
common_point_loss: Claiming continuity over an interval while ignoring holes, asymptotes, piecewise boundaries, or excluded domain values.

title: Removing Discontinuities
what_it_is: A removable discontinuity can be fixed by defining or redefining the function value so it equals the limit at that point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding the relevant limit and setting the function value or parameter equal to it.
answer_move: Find the limit at the discontinuity first, then set f(c) or the parameter expression equal to that limit.
common_point_loss: Solving for a value without showing that it matches the limiting behavior.

title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
what_it_is: An infinite limit describes function values growing without bound as x approaches a finite input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using limit notation to describe unbounded behavior and connecting it to a vertical asymptote when appropriate.
answer_move: Check each side of the input. If f(x) grows without bound, write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote.
common_point_loss: Writing only does not exist when the problem asks for behavior or an asymptote connection.

title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
what_it_is: A limit at infinity describes end behavior as x grows very large positive or negative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying end behavior, writing the correct limit at infinity, and connecting a finite result to y = L.
answer_move: Ask what f(x) approaches as x goes far left or far right. If it approaches L, name y = L.
common_point_loss: Confusing vertical asymptotes with horizontal asymptotes or finite-input limits with limits at infinity.

title: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem
what_it_is: The Intermediate Value Theorem says a continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values somewhere inside the interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by verifying continuity, showing the target value lies between endpoint values, and stating the existence conclusion.
answer_move: Write the conditions first: continuous on [a,b], target between f(a) and f(b), therefore some c exists in (a,b).
common_point_loss: Jumping to the conclusion without verifying continuity and the endpoint-value condition.

title: Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point
what_it_is: Average rate compares total change over an interval, while instantaneous rate describes the limiting rate at one input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing interval-based average rate from point-based instantaneous rate and by setting up the correct difference quotient or limiting interpretation.
answer_move: Name the quantity first: average over an interval or instantaneous at a point. Then use a secant slope or tangent-slope limit accordingly.
common_point_loss: Using the average rate formula when the question asks for the rate at one instant.

title: Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation
what_it_is: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing correct derivative notation, interpreting it in context, and connecting the derivative to a limit or slope.
answer_move: Translate f'(a) as the instantaneous rate of change of f with respect to x at x = a.
common_point_loss: Treating f'(a) as a y-value of the original function instead of as a rate or slope.

title: Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point
what_it_is: A derivative can be estimated from nearby graph or table values when an exact formula is not available.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing nearby points, computing a reasonable local rate, and labeling the estimate with units when the context has units.
answer_move: Use the closest available values around the point and describe the estimate as a local slope.
common_point_loss: Using distant data values or failing to distinguish an estimate from an exact derivative.

title: Connecting Differentiability and Continuity
what_it_is: Differentiability at a point means a derivative exists there, and differentiability implies continuity at that point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking whether the function is continuous and whether the local slope behavior has one consistent finite value.
answer_move: Use the chain: differentiable -> continuous. If continuity fails, differentiability fails too.
common_point_loss: Claiming a derivative exists at a corner or discontinuity because the graph has points on both sides.

title: Applying the Power Rule
what_it_is: The power rule differentiates x^n by multiplying by the exponent and reducing the exponent by one.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying the exponent change accurately, including negative and fractional powers after rewriting radicals or reciprocals.
answer_move: Rewrite the expression as powers of x first, then apply d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1).
common_point_loss: Dropping coefficients or mishandling negative and fractional exponents.

title: Derivative Rules: Constant, Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple
what_it_is: These rules let students differentiate expressions term by term while preserving coefficients and signs.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating terms correctly, carrying constants through the derivative, and making the derivative of a constant zero.
answer_move: Differentiate one term at a time and keep every coefficient and sign visible until the end.
common_point_loss: Forgetting that constants differentiate to zero or changing signs during term-by-term work.

title: Derivatives of cos x, sin x, e^x, and ln x
what_it_is: These are foundational derivative facts for trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recalling the correct base derivative and combining it with other rules when the expression is more complex.
answer_move: Identify the function family first, then apply its derivative fact before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Changing the sign of the trig derivative incorrectly or treating ln x like 1/x only after forgetting domain context.

title: The Product Rule
what_it_is: The product rule differentiates a product by differentiating each factor once while leaving the other factor unchanged.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing both product-rule terms and applying any needed inner derivative inside each factor.
answer_move: Write first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Differentiating both factors at once or omitting one of the two product-rule terms.

title: The Quotient Rule
what_it_is: The quotient rule differentiates a ratio by combining the derivative of the numerator and denominator over the denominator squared.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by preserving the quotient-rule order, squaring the denominator, and simplifying only after the derivative structure is correct.
answer_move: Use low d-high minus high d-low over low squared, then check signs before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Reversing the numerator terms or forgetting to square the denominator.

title: Derivatives of tan x, cot x, sec x, and csc x
what_it_is: These derivative facts extend trig differentiation beyond sine and cosine.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recalling the correct trig derivative and sign, then combining it with product, quotient, or chain rule structure if needed.
answer_move: Pair each trig function with its derivative fact before doing any algebraic simplification.
common_point_loss: Mixing up the signs for cot x and csc x or confusing sec x tan x with sec^2 x.

title: The Chain Rule
what_it_is: The chain rule differentiates composite functions by multiplying the derivative of the outside function by the derivative of the inside function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying inside and outside functions and including the inner derivative factor.
answer_move: Circle the inside expression, differentiate the outside around it, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
common_point_loss: Differentiating the outside function but forgetting the inner derivative.

title: Implicit Differentiation
what_it_is: Implicit differentiation finds dy/dx when x and y are related by an equation that is not solved for y.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating both sides with respect to x and attaching dy/dx whenever differentiating a y-expression.
answer_move: Differentiate term by term, mark every y-derivative with dy/dx, then solve algebraically for dy/dx.
common_point_loss: Forgetting the dy/dx factor on terms involving y.

title: Differentiating Inverse Functions
what_it_is: The derivative of an inverse function is tied to the reciprocal of the derivative of the original function at the corresponding point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching the inverse input to the original output and using the reciprocal derivative at the matching original input.
answer_move: Find the point on f that corresponds to the inverse input, then take 1/f'(that x-value).
common_point_loss: Using the reciprocal at the wrong x-value or confusing f inverse with 1/f.

title: Differentiating Inverse Trigonometric Functions
what_it_is: Inverse trigonometric derivatives have specific algebraic forms that often combine with the chain rule.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by selecting the correct inverse trig derivative formula and applying the inner derivative when the argument is not just x.
answer_move: Identify the inverse trig function, write its derivative template, then substitute the inside expression and multiply by its derivative.
common_point_loss: Forgetting the chain rule or confusing arcsin, arctan, and arcsec denominator forms.

title: Selecting Procedures for Calculating Derivatives
what_it_is: This topic is about choosing which derivative rule or combination of rules fits the structure of a function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching product, quotient, chain, implicit, or basic rules to the expression before calculating.
answer_move: Pause before differentiating and name the outer structure: sum, product, quotient, composition, or implicit relation.
common_point_loss: Applying a familiar rule to the whole expression without checking the actual structure.

title: Calculating Higher-Order Derivatives
what_it_is: Higher-order derivatives are derivatives of derivatives, such as second derivative and beyond.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating repeatedly while keeping notation clear and interpreting each derivative in context when asked.
answer_move: Compute one derivative at a time and label f', f'', or the requested order before substituting values.
common_point_loss: Substituting too early or losing track of which derivative the question asks for.

title: Interpreting the Meaning of the Derivative in Context
what_it_is: A derivative in context is a rate of change with units and a specific meaning tied to the quantities in the problem.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by stating what is changing, with respect to what, at what input, and in what units.
answer_move: Use the sentence frame: at x = a, the quantity is changing at about/value units of output per unit of input.
common_point_loss: Giving a numeric derivative without units or contextual meaning.

title: Straight-Line Motion: Connecting Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
what_it_is: Position, velocity, and acceleration are connected by derivatives: velocity is position's derivative and acceleration is velocity's derivative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct derivative relationship and interpreting sign and magnitude in the context of motion.
answer_move: Write the chain s(t) -> v(t) -> a(t), then decide whether the question asks for position, direction, speed, or acceleration.
common_point_loss: Confusing velocity with speed or treating negative velocity as slower instead of direction-dependent.

title: Rates of Change in Applied Contexts Other Than Motion
what_it_is: Derivatives describe rates in contexts such as volume, population, temperature, cost, and concentration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the dependent and independent variables and expressing the derivative as a contextual rate.
answer_move: Translate dy/dx as change in y per change in x, then attach the problem's units.
common_point_loss: Writing a derivative symbol or value without saying what real-world rate it represents.

title: Introduction to Related Rates
what_it_is: Related rates problems connect multiple changing quantities through an equation and differentiate with respect to time.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining variables, writing the relationship before differentiating, and distinguishing known rates from the requested rate.
answer_move: Draw or define the variables, write the equation, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute known values.
common_point_loss: Substituting values before differentiating or mixing up variables with their rates.

title: Solving Related Rates Problems
what_it_is: Solving related rates means carrying the setup through implicit differentiation and algebra to find the requested rate.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing the model equation, differentiating correctly, substituting time-specific values, and answering with units.
answer_move: Keep d/dt visible through the differentiation step, then plug in the snapshot values after the derivative equation is formed.
common_point_loss: Answering for the wrong rate or using a value that belongs to a different time.

title: Approximating Values of a Function Using Local Linearity and Linearization
what_it_is: Linearization uses the tangent line near a point to approximate nearby function values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by building L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a), substituting the nearby input, and stating that it is an approximation.
answer_move: Find f(a) and f'(a), write the tangent-line model, then evaluate the nearby x-value.
common_point_loss: Using a secant line or forgetting that the approximation is anchored at the given point a.

title: Using L'Hospital's Rule for Determining Limits of Indeterminate Forms
what_it_is: L'Hospital's Rule evaluates certain indeterminate limits by comparing derivatives of numerator and denominator.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by first verifying an indeterminate form such as 0/0 or infinity/infinity, then differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
answer_move: State the indeterminate form, apply L'Hospital's Rule, then evaluate the new limit.
common_point_loss: Applying the rule without verifying the form or using quotient rule instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately.

title: Using the Mean Value Theorem
what_it_is: The Mean Value Theorem connects an average rate over an interval to at least one matching instantaneous rate inside the interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking continuity and differentiability conditions, computing the average rate, and stating the guaranteed c-value conclusion.
answer_move: Verify conditions first, then set f'(c) equal to the secant slope.
common_point_loss: Using the theorem without stating continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.

title: Extreme Value Theorem, Global Versus Local Extrema, and Critical Points
what_it_is: This topic distinguishes absolute extrema, local extrema, and critical points where extrema may occur.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding critical points, considering endpoints when needed, and using the correct vocabulary for local versus absolute behavior.
answer_move: List candidates from critical points and endpoints, then compare values if the question asks for absolute extrema.
common_point_loss: Ignoring endpoints or calling every critical point a maximum or minimum.

title: Determining Intervals on Which a Function Is Increasing or Decreasing
what_it_is: A function increases where its derivative is positive and decreases where its derivative is negative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by testing derivative sign on intervals and translating that sign into increasing or decreasing behavior.
answer_move: Make a sign chart for f' and state intervals using x-values, not y-values.
common_point_loss: Using f-values instead of derivative signs to decide increasing or decreasing intervals.

title: Using the First Derivative Test
what_it_is: The first derivative test classifies local extrema by how f' changes sign around a critical point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing f' changes from positive to negative for a local maximum or negative to positive for a local minimum.
answer_move: Check f' on the left and right of the critical point before naming the extremum.
common_point_loss: Saying f'(c)=0 is enough to prove a maximum or minimum.

title: Using the Candidates Test to Determine Absolute Extrema
what_it_is: The candidates test compares function values at endpoints and critical points to identify absolute extrema on a closed interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying all candidates, evaluating the original function at each one, and selecting the largest or smallest value.
answer_move: Build a candidates table: endpoints plus interior critical points, then compare f-values.
common_point_loss: Comparing derivative values instead of function values or omitting endpoints.

title: Determining Concavity
what_it_is: Concavity describes whether slopes are increasing or decreasing and is determined by the sign of the second derivative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding where f'' is positive or negative and translating that sign into concave up or concave down intervals.
answer_move: Make a sign chart for f'' and state concavity on intervals.
common_point_loss: Using f' sign to decide concavity instead of f'' sign.

title: Using the Second Derivative Test
what_it_is: The second derivative test can classify certain critical points using the sign of f'' at the point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by confirming f'(c)=0 or undefined as needed and then using f''(c) to classify the local behavior when possible.
answer_move: Check the critical point first, then use f''(c)>0 for local minimum or f''(c)<0 for local maximum.
common_point_loss: Using the test when f''(c)=0 and treating an inconclusive result as a conclusion.

title: Sketching Graphs of Functions and Their Derivatives
what_it_is: Graph sketching connects function values, derivative signs, slope behavior, extrema, and concavity into one representation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using derivative evidence to place increasing/decreasing intervals, extrema, concavity, and inflection behavior correctly.
answer_move: Annotate the derivative evidence first, then sketch only what the evidence supports.
common_point_loss: Drawing a graph from intuition without tying features to derivative sign or second-derivative sign.

title: Connecting a Function, Its First Derivative, and Its Second Derivative
what_it_is: This topic asks students to translate among f, f', and f'' in graphs, tables, and symbolic forms.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting f' to slope and f'' to change in slope, then using those links to justify behavior.
answer_move: Ask which graph or table represents values, slopes, or changes in slopes before answering.
common_point_loss: Confusing the graph of f with the graph of f' when identifying extrema or concavity.

title: Introduction to Optimization Problems
what_it_is: Optimization uses derivatives to find maximum or minimum values of a quantity under given constraints.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the quantity to optimize, writing it as a one-variable function, and identifying the relevant domain.
answer_move: Define variables, write the objective function, use the constraint to reduce to one variable, then state the domain.
common_point_loss: Differentiating before creating a valid one-variable objective function.

title: Solving Optimization Problems
what_it_is: Solving optimization problems means finding candidates, testing them, and interpreting the best value in context.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the objective, finding critical points in the domain, justifying max or min, and answering the contextual question.
answer_move: After setup, solve f'(x)=0, test candidates, then answer with units and the requested variable.
common_point_loss: Finding a critical point but not proving it gives the requested maximum or minimum.

title: Exploring Behaviors of Implicit Relations
what_it_is: Implicit relations can have slopes, extrema, and concavity even when they are not written as y = f(x).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using implicit differentiation to obtain dy/dx and then applying behavior rules to the relation.
answer_move: Differentiate implicitly, solve for dy/dx, then evaluate slope or behavior at the specified point.
common_point_loss: Trying to treat y as a constant or assuming the relation is already solved for y.

title: Exploring Accumulations of Change
what_it_is: Accumulation describes how small changes add up over an interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by interpreting a rate over an interval as accumulated change and connecting area under a rate graph to total amount.
answer_move: Identify the rate, identify the interval, then describe the accumulation as total change over that interval.
common_point_loss: Treating the rate value at one point as the accumulated total over an interval.

title: Approximating Areas with Riemann Sums
what_it_is: Riemann sums approximate accumulated area using rectangles based on left, right, midpoint, or other sample values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the correct subinterval widths and sample heights, then summing width times height with units.
answer_move: For each subinterval, compute base times chosen height, then add the products.
common_point_loss: Using the wrong endpoint or assuming all subintervals have equal width when they do not.

title: Riemann Sums, Summation Notation, and Definite Integral Notation
what_it_is: This topic connects rectangle sums, sigma notation, and definite integrals as representations of accumulated change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching limits of integration, subinterval structure, and integrand meaning to the accumulation being represented.
answer_move: Translate the notation into total accumulation from a to b of the rate or height function.
common_point_loss: Misreading the bounds or treating definite integral notation as an antiderivative request only.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Accumulation Functions
what_it_is: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links accumulation functions to derivatives of their integrands.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing that the derivative of an accumulation function depends on the integrand and any variable bound behavior.
answer_move: For F(x)=integral from a to x of f(t)dt, write F'(x)=f(x); adjust with chain rule if the bound is not x.
common_point_loss: Replacing the accumulation function with a number or forgetting the chain rule for variable bounds.

title: Interpreting the Behavior of Accumulation Functions
what_it_is: Accumulation functions increase or decrease based on the sign of the rate being accumulated, and their concavity depends on how that rate changes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting the integrand to the derivative of the accumulation function and then reasoning about sign or slope.
answer_move: Treat the integrand as F'(x), then use derivative-sign logic to discuss F.
common_point_loss: Judging the accumulation function directly from the area picture without using the integrand as its derivative.

title: Applying Properties of Definite Integrals
what_it_is: Definite integral properties allow students to split, combine, reverse, and scale accumulated quantities.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying interval additivity, sign reversal, constant multiples, and symmetry when appropriate.
answer_move: Rewrite the requested integral in terms of known intervals or areas before calculating.
common_point_loss: Adding areas without accounting for sign or reversed bounds.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Definite Integrals
what_it_is: The evaluation part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus uses antiderivatives to compute exact definite integrals.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding a valid antiderivative, evaluating it at the bounds, and subtracting upper minus lower.
answer_move: Find F, then compute F(b)-F(a) and attach contextual units when the integral represents change.
common_point_loss: Subtracting in the wrong order or forgetting that a definite integral can be negative when it represents signed change.

title: Finding Antiderivatives and Indefinite Integrals
what_it_is: An antiderivative reverses differentiation, and an indefinite integral represents a family of functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using correct reverse derivative rules and including +C for indefinite integrals.
answer_move: Ask what function would differentiate to this expression, then include the constant of integration when no bounds are present.
common_point_loss: Forgetting +C or applying derivative rules forward instead of reversing them.

title: Integrating Using Substitution
what_it_is: Substitution reverses the chain rule by changing variables so a composite integrand becomes simpler.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing u, computing du, rewriting the integral consistently, and adjusting bounds for definite integrals when used.
answer_move: Choose the inside expression as u, find du, rewrite everything in u, then integrate.
common_point_loss: Leaving a mix of x and u in the same integral or forgetting to adjust definite bounds.

title: Integrating Functions Using Long Division and Completing the Square
what_it_is: Some rational expressions must be rewritten by long division or completing the square before integration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by rewriting the integrand into an equivalent form and then applying the appropriate antiderivative rule.
answer_move: When the integral does not match a basic form, rewrite the algebra first, then integrate the simpler pieces.
common_point_loss: Trying to integrate a complicated rational expression directly without making the needed algebraic rewrite.

title: Selecting Techniques for Antidifferentiation
what_it_is: This topic is about choosing a valid integration method based on the structure of the integrand.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching the integrand structure to an antidifferentiation procedure before calculating.
answer_move: Classify the integrand first: basic reverse rule, composite needing substitution, rational needing rewrite, or product needing another technique.
common_point_loss: Forcing substitution or a memorized pattern when the integrand structure points elsewhere.

title: Modeling Situations with Differential Equations
what_it_is: Differential equations model situations where a quantity's rate of change depends on variables in the situation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by translating verbal rate relationships into equations involving dy/dx or related notation.
answer_move: Identify the quantity, identify what controls its rate, then write the differential equation with the correct variables.
common_point_loss: Writing a formula for y instead of an equation for the rate of change.

title: Verifying Solutions for Differential Equations
what_it_is: A proposed solution satisfies a differential equation if its derivative matches the rate expression after substitution.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the proposed solution and comparing it to the right-hand side of the differential equation.
answer_move: Compute dy/dx from the proposed y, substitute y and x into the differential equation, then show they match.
common_point_loss: Checking only the initial condition or only the equation, rather than verifying both when both are asked.

title: Sketching Slope Fields
what_it_is: A slope field shows small line segments whose slopes come from a differential equation at points in the plane.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by computing slopes at specified points and drawing segments with correct relative direction and steepness.
answer_move: Plug each point into dy/dx, then draw a short segment with that slope at the point.
common_point_loss: Drawing solution curves when the task asks for field segments, or ignoring the sign of the slope.

title: Reasoning Using Slope Fields
what_it_is: Slope fields allow students to infer solution behavior, equilibrium behavior, and approximate paths from local slopes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting the displayed segment slopes to whether solutions increase, decrease, level off, or change direction.
answer_move: Follow the local directions of the field and describe the solution curve consistent with nearby slopes.
common_point_loss: Reading the slope field as a graph of y-values rather than as directions for solution curves.

title: Finding General Solutions Using Separation of Variables
what_it_is: Separation of variables solves certain differential equations by placing y terms with dy and x terms with dx before integrating.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating variables correctly, integrating both sides, and including the constant of integration.
answer_move: Move all y terms to one side and x terms to the other, integrate, then include +C.
common_point_loss: Mixing x and y after separation or omitting the integration constant.

title: Finding Particular Solutions Using Initial Conditions and Separation of Variables
what_it_is: A particular solution uses an initial condition to determine the constant in a general differential equation solution.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by solving generally, substituting the initial condition, determining C, and presenting the particular solution.
answer_move: Do not wait until the end mentally: substitute the given point clearly to solve for C.
common_point_loss: Leaving the answer with an undetermined C or applying the initial condition to the derivative instead of the solution.

title: Exponential Models with Differential Equations
what_it_is: Exponential models arise when a quantity changes at a rate proportional to the quantity itself.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing dy/dt = ky structure and interpreting the sign and meaning of k in context.
answer_move: Look for rate proportional to amount, then write or use the exponential solution model with the initial value.
common_point_loss: Using a linear model when the rate depends on the current amount.

title: Finding the Average Value of a Function on an Interval
what_it_is: Average value uses a definite integral divided by interval length to find the function's mean height over an interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by setting up 1/(b-a) times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx and interpreting the result with correct units.
answer_move: Write the formula before evaluating so the interval length and integral are both visible.
common_point_loss: Confusing average value with slope between endpoints.

title: Connecting Position, Velocity, and Acceleration Using Integrals
what_it_is: Integrals connect velocity to change in position and acceleration to change in velocity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using definite integrals to compute displacement or change in velocity and by distinguishing displacement from distance traveled.
answer_move: Identify whether the integral of velocity gives displacement or whether total distance requires integrating speed.
common_point_loss: Reporting displacement when the question asks for total distance traveled.

title: Using Accumulation Functions and Definite Integrals in Applied Contexts
what_it_is: Definite integrals in context accumulate rates into total change for quantities like volume, population, temperature, or cost.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the rate, integrating over the correct interval, and adding an initial value when the question asks for an amount.
answer_move: Use final amount = initial amount + accumulated change when an initial value is given.
common_point_loss: Forgetting the initial amount or attaching the rate's units instead of the accumulated quantity's units.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves Expressed as Functions of x
what_it_is: Area between x-functions uses vertical slices and integrates top function minus bottom function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding intersection bounds and integrating upper minus lower over each interval.
answer_move: Sketch or compare functions to identify top and bottom, then integrate top minus bottom with respect to x.
common_point_loss: Reversing top and bottom or failing to split intervals when the top function changes.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves Expressed as Functions of y
what_it_is: Area between y-functions uses horizontal slices and integrates right function minus left function with respect to y.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using y-bounds and subtracting left from right in the horizontal-slice setup.
answer_move: Identify rightmost x and leftmost x as functions of y, then integrate right minus left dy.
common_point_loss: Using dx bounds or top-minus-bottom logic when the setup requires horizontal slices.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves That Intersect at More Than Two Points
what_it_is: When curves intersect more than twice, the region may need to be split into intervals with different top-bottom relationships.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying all relevant intersection points, splitting the region, and using the correct subtraction order on each interval.
answer_move: Find every intersection, draw or test each interval, then add the separate area integrals.
common_point_loss: Using one integral across the whole interval when the upper and lower functions switch.

title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Squares and Rectangles
what_it_is: Cross-section volume sums areas of slices whose square or rectangular dimensions are based on a region in the base.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the slice width, writing the cross-sectional area formula, and integrating that area over the correct bounds.
answer_move: Base of slice from the region first, area formula second, integral of area last.
common_point_loss: Integrating a length instead of an area or using the wrong side length for the cross section.

title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Triangles and Semicircles
what_it_is: Triangular and semicircular cross sections use geometry formulas to turn base lengths into slice areas.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the cross-section shape, substituting the region's base length into the correct area formula, and integrating.
answer_move: Write the shape formula before substituting the base length from the graph or equations.
common_point_loss: Using square cross-section area when the problem specifies triangles or semicircles.

title: Volume with Disc Method: Revolving Around the x- or y-Axis
what_it_is: The disc method finds volume by integrating circular cross-sectional areas when a region rotates around a coordinate axis without a hole.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the radius perpendicular to the axis of rotation and integrating pi times radius squared over the correct bounds.
answer_move: Draw the radius from the axis to the curve, then write pi r^2 for the slice area.
common_point_loss: Using diameter as radius or choosing a radius parallel to the axis of rotation.

title: Volume with Disc Method: Revolving Around Other Axes
what_it_is: Disc method around a non-coordinate axis still uses circular slices, but the radius is a distance to the given line of rotation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by expressing the radius as the distance from the curve to the rotation axis and integrating pi r^2.
answer_move: Write radius = distance to axis, then square it inside pi r^2.
common_point_loss: Using f(x) as the radius when the axis is shifted away from the coordinate axis.

title: Volume with Washer Method: Revolving Around the x- or y-Axis
what_it_is: The washer method finds volume when rotation creates an outer radius and an inner radius.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying both radii and integrating pi times outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
answer_move: Draw both distances from the axis, label outer and inner, then write pi(R^2-r^2).
common_point_loss: Subtracting radii before squaring or reversing inner and outer radii.

title: Volume with Washer Method: Revolving Around Other Axes
what_it_is: Washer method around a shifted axis uses outer and inner radii measured as distances to that axis.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining both shifted-axis distances and preserving the pi(R^2-r^2) structure.
answer_move: Measure each radius from the rotation line, not from the coordinate axis, then subtract areas.
common_point_loss: Forgetting to adjust radii for the shifted axis.

title: Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?
what_it_is: This topic introduces the move from average change over an interval to change at a single instant. A limit describes what average rates approach as the interval around the instant shrinks.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing whether a question asks about an interval or an instant and by connecting the instant case to limiting behavior.
answer_move: Ask: over an interval or at one point? If it is at one point, describe the instantaneous rate as the value approached by average rates over smaller intervals.
common_point_loss: Trying to compute an instantaneous rate as a direct quotient with zero change in x.

title: Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation
what_it_is: A limit describes the value a function approaches as x gets close to a chosen input. Limit notation names that approaching behavior precisely.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading and writing the approaching input, function, direction when specified, and value approached.
answer_move: Read the notation as: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L. Keep approaches separate from equals.
common_point_loss: Replacing the limit with f(a) automatically, or dropping the direction marker on a one-sided limit.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Graphs
what_it_is: A graph can show what y-value a function approaches as x moves toward a chosen input from the left, right, or both sides.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying left-hand and right-hand behavior and concluding whether the two-sided limit exists.
answer_move: Trace the graph toward the x-value from both sides before looking at the point on the graph.
common_point_loss: Using a filled or open point as the limit value without checking nearby graph behavior.

title: Estimating Limit Values from Tables
what_it_is: A table can suggest a limit by showing how function values behave for x-values close to a chosen input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using nearby table values from both sides and writing an estimate that matches the evidence.
answer_move: Look inward from both sides of the table, then state the trend and estimated limit.
common_point_loss: Choosing one table entry instead of describing the trend across nearby entries.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits
what_it_is: Limit properties let students combine simpler limits to determine limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and composite functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying a valid property, preserving expression structure, and showing setup that makes the final value follow.
answer_move: Break the expression into parts, determine component limits, then apply the matching property.
common_point_loss: Applying quotient or composition rules mechanically when the needed conditions are not met.

title: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation
what_it_is: Some limit expressions hide their behavior until they are rewritten into an equivalent useful form.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing a valid rewrite, showing the transformed expression, and evaluating from the simplified form.
answer_move: When substitution is blocked, ask what equivalent form removes the obstacle.
common_point_loss: Stopping at 0/0, or canceling terms that are not common factors.

title: Selecting Procedures for Determining Limits
what_it_is: This topic is about choosing the method that fits the limit problem before carrying out the calculation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by classifying the problem form and selecting a procedure that matches it.
answer_move: Before solving, name the cue: direct substitution works, sides must be checked, factoring helps, or another strategy fits.
common_point_loss: Defaulting to a familiar technique without checking whether the problem calls for it.

title: Determining Limits Using the Squeeze Theorem
what_it_is: The squeeze theorem finds a limit by trapping one function between two functions that approach the same value.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing bounds, showing both bounding limits match, and then stating the squeezed conclusion.
answer_move: Write the inequality first, find the outside limits, then conclude the middle limit.
common_point_loss: Naming the theorem without showing the bounding relationship and matching limits.

title: Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits
what_it_is: The same limit can be represented by notation, words, a graph, a table, or an equation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the same limiting behavior across representations and keeping the claim consistent.
answer_move: Convert each representation into: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L.
