common_point_loss: Matching a table or graph to a function value instead of to approach behavior.

title: Exploring Types of Discontinuities
what_it_is: A discontinuity is a place where continuity fails. The type depends on whether the value, one-sided limits, or bounded behavior fails.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by classifying the discontinuity and connecting that classification to limit evidence.
answer_move: Check left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and f(c), then classify based on which part fails.
common_point_loss: Calling every gap removable or every discontinuity an asymptote without checking behavior.

title: Defining Continuity at a Point
what_it_is: A function is continuous at a point when f(c) exists, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(c).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking all three conditions and using them to justify whether the function is continuous.
answer_move: Use the checklist: value exists, limit exists, value equals limit, then state the conclusion.
common_point_loss: Saying a function is continuous because the graph looks connected without verifying conditions.

title: Confirming Continuity over an Interval
what_it_is: Continuity over an interval means the function is continuous at every point in that interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the interval, checking special points, and naming domain restrictions or endpoints that matter.
answer_move: Start with the function family and domain, then check special points inside the interval.
common_point_loss: Claiming continuity over an interval while ignoring holes, asymptotes, piecewise boundaries, or excluded domain values.

title: Removing Discontinuities
what_it_is: A removable discontinuity can be fixed by defining or redefining the function value so it equals the limit at that point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding the relevant limit and setting the function value or parameter equal to it.
answer_move: Find the limit at the discontinuity first, then set f(c) or the parameter expression equal to that limit.
common_point_loss: Solving for a value without showing that it matches the limiting behavior.

title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
what_it_is: An infinite limit describes function values growing without bound as x approaches a finite input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using limit notation to describe unbounded behavior and connecting it to a vertical asymptote when appropriate.
answer_move: Check each side of the input. If f(x) grows without bound, write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote.
common_point_loss: Writing only does not exist when the problem asks for behavior or an asymptote connection.

title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
what_it_is: A limit at infinity describes end behavior as x grows very large positive or negative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying end behavior, writing the correct limit at infinity, and connecting a finite result to y = L.
answer_move: Ask what f(x) approaches as x goes far left or far right. If it approaches L, name y = L.
common_point_loss: Confusing vertical asymptotes with horizontal asymptotes or finite-input limits with limits at infinity.

title: Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem
what_it_is: The Intermediate Value Theorem says a continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values somewhere inside the interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by verifying continuity, showing the target value lies between endpoint values, and stating the existence conclusion.
answer_move: Write the conditions first: continuous on [a,b], target between f(a) and f(b), therefore some c exists in (a,b).
common_point_loss: Jumping to the conclusion without verifying continuity and the endpoint-value condition.

title: Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point
what_it_is: Average rate compares total change over an interval, while instantaneous rate describes the limiting rate at one input.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing interval-based average rate from point-based instantaneous rate and by setting up the correct difference quotient or limiting interpretation.
answer_move: Name the quantity first: average over an interval or instantaneous at a point. Then use a secant slope or tangent-slope limit accordingly.
common_point_loss: Using the average rate formula when the question asks for the rate at one instant.

title: Defining the Derivative of a Function and Using Derivative Notation
what_it_is: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing correct derivative notation, interpreting it in context, and connecting the derivative to a limit or slope.
answer_move: Translate f'(a) as the instantaneous rate of change of f with respect to x at x = a.
common_point_loss: Treating f'(a) as a y-value of the original function instead of as a rate or slope.

title: Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point
what_it_is: A derivative can be estimated from nearby graph or table values when an exact formula is not available.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing nearby points, computing a reasonable local rate, and labeling the estimate with units when the context has units.
answer_move: Use the closest available values around the point and describe the estimate as a local slope.
common_point_loss: Using distant data values or failing to distinguish an estimate from an exact derivative.

title: Connecting Differentiability and Continuity
what_it_is: Differentiability at a point means a derivative exists there, and differentiability implies continuity at that point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking whether the function is continuous and whether the local slope behavior has one consistent finite value.
answer_move: Use the chain: differentiable -> continuous. If continuity fails, differentiability fails too.
common_point_loss: Claiming a derivative exists at a corner or discontinuity because the graph has points on both sides.

title: Applying the Power Rule
what_it_is: The power rule differentiates x^n by multiplying by the exponent and reducing the exponent by one.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying the exponent change accurately, including negative and fractional powers after rewriting radicals or reciprocals.
answer_move: Rewrite the expression as powers of x first, then apply d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1).
common_point_loss: Dropping coefficients or mishandling negative and fractional exponents.

title: Derivative Rules: Constant, Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple
what_it_is: These rules let students differentiate expressions term by term while preserving coefficients and signs.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating terms correctly, carrying constants through the derivative, and making the derivative of a constant zero.
answer_move: Differentiate one term at a time and keep every coefficient and sign visible until the end.
common_point_loss: Forgetting that constants differentiate to zero or changing signs during term-by-term work.

title: Derivatives of cos x, sin x, e^x, and ln x
what_it_is: These are foundational derivative facts for trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recalling the correct base derivative and combining it with other rules when the expression is more complex.
answer_move: Identify the function family first, then apply its derivative fact before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Changing the sign of the trig derivative incorrectly or treating ln x like 1/x only after forgetting domain context.

title: The Product Rule
what_it_is: The product rule differentiates a product by differentiating each factor once while leaving the other factor unchanged.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing both product-rule terms and applying any needed inner derivative inside each factor.
answer_move: Write first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Differentiating both factors at once or omitting one of the two product-rule terms.

title: The Quotient Rule
what_it_is: The quotient rule differentiates a ratio by combining the derivative of the numerator and denominator over the denominator squared.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by preserving the quotient-rule order, squaring the denominator, and simplifying only after the derivative structure is correct.
answer_move: Use low d-high minus high d-low over low squared, then check signs before simplifying.
common_point_loss: Reversing the numerator terms or forgetting to square the denominator.

title: Derivatives of tan x, cot x, sec x, and csc x
what_it_is: These derivative facts extend trig differentiation beyond sine and cosine.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recalling the correct trig derivative and sign, then combining it with product, quotient, or chain rule structure if needed.
answer_move: Pair each trig function with its derivative fact before doing any algebraic simplification.
common_point_loss: Mixing up the signs for cot x and csc x or confusing sec x tan x with sec^2 x.

title: The Chain Rule
what_it_is: The chain rule differentiates a composite function f(g(x)) by multiplying the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inner function, by the derivative of the inner function itself.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by correctly identifying which piece is the outer function and which is the inner function, and by explicitly multiplying by the inner function's derivative rather than stopping after the outer function.
answer_move: Identify the outer function and the inner function separately, differentiate the outer function and evaluate it at the inner function, then multiply the result by the inner function's own derivative.
common_point_loss: Differentiating the outer function correctly but forgetting to multiply by the inner function's derivative, or misidentifying which piece is the inner function.

title: Implicit Differentiation
what_it_is: Implicit differentiation finds dy/dx from an equation relating x and y that is not solved for y, by differentiating both sides with respect to x and treating y as a function of x via the chain rule.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by attaching dy/dx correctly to every y-term via the chain rule, collecting dy/dx terms with parentheses around any coefficient, and, for a vertical-tangent question, setting the denominator, not the numerator, of dy/dx equal to zero.
answer_move: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, attach dy/dx to every y-term, collect dy/dx terms with parentheses around the coefficient, then solve; for a vertical tangent, set the denominator equal to zero, not the numerator.
common_point_loss: Setting the numerator of dy/dx equal to zero, the horizontal-tangent condition, when the question actually asks for a vertical tangent, which requires the denominator equal to zero.

title: Differentiating Inverse Functions
what_it_is: If g is the inverse of f, then g'(x) equals the reciprocal of f'(g(x)) -- the derivative of the inverse at a point is tied to the derivative of the original function evaluated at the corresponding swapped point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by correctly identifying the corresponding point on the original function, swapping x and y from the point given for the inverse, before taking the reciprocal of that derivative value.
answer_move: If asked for g'(a) where g is the inverse of f, first find the point b such that f(b) = a, then compute g'(a) as 1 divided by f'(b).
common_point_loss: Taking the reciprocal of f'(a) directly instead of first finding the corresponding input b where f(b) = a.

title: Differentiating Inverse Trigonometric Functions
what_it_is: Each inverse trigonometric function has its own specific derivative formula, for example the derivative of arcsin(x) is 1 over the square root of 1 minus x squared, distinct from the derivatives of sine, cosine, or tangent themselves.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by citing the correct inverse-trig derivative formula, not a regular trig derivative, and applying the chain rule correctly when the inverse-trig function's argument is itself a function of x.
answer_move: Identify which inverse-trig function is present, recall its specific derivative formula, then apply the chain rule if its argument is more than just x.
common_point_loss: Reaching for the derivative of sine, cosine, or tangent instead of the distinct inverse-trig derivative formula.

title: Selecting Procedures for Calculating Derivatives
what_it_is: This topic is about recognizing which derivative rule or combination of rules -- product, quotient, chain, implicit, inverse, or inverse-trig -- fits a given function's structure before differentiating.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by correctly classifying the function's structure and naming the matching procedure before carrying out any differentiation.
answer_move: Before differentiating, ask whether the expression is a product of two functions, a quotient, a composition, an implicit relationship, or an inverse function, and name the matching rule.
common_point_loss: Using the product rule on an expression that is actually a composition requiring the chain rule.

title: Calculating Higher-Order Derivatives
what_it_is: Higher-order derivatives are found by differentiating repeatedly -- the second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative, the third is the derivative of the second, and so on.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the correct number of times for what the question actually asks, and by correctly interpreting what a second derivative means in context, such as acceleration or concavity, when asked.
answer_move: Identify how many times you need to differentiate based on what is being asked (velocity needs one derivative of position, acceleration needs two), then differentiate that many times.
common_point_loss: Stopping after the first derivative when the question asks for acceleration, concavity, or another second-derivative quantity.

title: Interpreting the Meaning of the Derivative in Context
what_it_is: A derivative in context is a rate of change with units and a specific meaning tied to the quantities in the problem.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by stating what is changing, with respect to what, at what input, and in what units.
answer_move: Use the sentence frame: at x = a, the quantity is changing at about/value units of output per unit of input.
common_point_loss: Giving a numeric derivative without units or contextual meaning.

title: Straight-Line Motion: Connecting Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
what_it_is: Position, velocity, and acceleration are connected by derivatives: velocity is position's derivative and acceleration is velocity's derivative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct derivative relationship and interpreting sign and magnitude in the context of motion.
answer_move: Write the chain s(t) -> v(t) -> a(t), then decide whether the question asks for position, direction, speed, or acceleration.
common_point_loss: Confusing velocity with speed or treating negative velocity as slower instead of direction-dependent.

title: Rates of Change in Applied Contexts Other Than Motion
what_it_is: Derivatives describe rates in contexts such as volume, population, temperature, cost, and concentration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the dependent and independent variables and expressing the derivative as a contextual rate.
answer_move: Translate dy/dx as change in y per change in x, then attach the problem's units.
common_point_loss: Writing a derivative symbol or value without saying what real-world rate it represents.

title: Introduction to Related Rates
what_it_is: Related rates problems connect multiple changing quantities through an equation and differentiate with respect to time.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining variables, writing the relationship before differentiating, and distinguishing known rates from the requested rate.
answer_move: Draw or define the variables, write the equation, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute known values.
common_point_loss: Substituting values before differentiating or mixing up variables with their rates.

title: Solving Related Rates Problems
what_it_is: Solving related rates means carrying the setup through implicit differentiation and algebra to find the requested rate.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing the model equation, differentiating correctly, substituting time-specific values, and answering with units.
answer_move: Keep d/dt visible through the differentiation step, then plug in the snapshot values after the derivative equation is formed.
common_point_loss: Answering for the wrong rate or using a value that belongs to a different time.

title: Approximating Values of a Function Using Local Linearity and Linearization
what_it_is: Linearization uses the tangent line near a point to approximate nearby function values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by building L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a), substituting the nearby input, and stating that it is an approximation.
answer_move: Find f(a) and f'(a), write the tangent-line model, then evaluate the nearby x-value.
common_point_loss: Using a secant line or forgetting that the approximation is anchored at the given point a.

title: Using L'Hospital's Rule for Determining Limits of Indeterminate Forms
what_it_is: L'Hospital's Rule evaluates certain indeterminate limits by comparing derivatives of numerator and denominator.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by first verifying an indeterminate form such as 0/0 or infinity/infinity, then differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
answer_move: State the indeterminate form, apply L'Hospital's Rule, then evaluate the new limit.
common_point_loss: Applying the rule without verifying the form or using quotient rule instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately.

title: Using the Mean Value Theorem
what_it_is: The Mean Value Theorem connects an average rate over an interval to at least one matching instantaneous rate inside the interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking continuity and differentiability conditions, computing the average rate, and stating the guaranteed c-value conclusion.
answer_move: Verify conditions first, then set f'(c) equal to the secant slope.
common_point_loss: Using the theorem without stating continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.

title: Extreme Value Theorem, Global Versus Local Extrema, and Critical Points
what_it_is: This topic distinguishes absolute extrema, local extrema, and critical points where extrema may occur.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding critical points, considering endpoints when needed, and using the correct vocabulary for local versus absolute behavior.
answer_move: List candidates from critical points and endpoints, then compare values if the question asks for absolute extrema.
common_point_loss: Ignoring endpoints or calling every critical point a maximum or minimum.

title: Determining Intervals on Which a Function Is Increasing or Decreasing
what_it_is: A function increases where its derivative is positive and decreases where its derivative is negative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by testing derivative sign on intervals and translating that sign into increasing or decreasing behavior.
answer_move: Make a sign chart for f' and state intervals using x-values, not y-values.
common_point_loss: Using f-values instead of derivative signs to decide increasing or decreasing intervals.

title: Using the First Derivative Test
what_it_is: The first derivative test classifies local extrema by how f' changes sign around a critical point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing f' changes from positive to negative for a local maximum or negative to positive for a local minimum.
answer_move: Check f' on the left and right of the critical point before naming the extremum.
common_point_loss: Saying f'(c)=0 is enough to prove a maximum or minimum.

title: Using the Candidates Test to Determine Absolute Extrema
what_it_is: The candidates test compares function values at endpoints and critical points to identify absolute extrema on a closed interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying all candidates, evaluating the original function at each one, and selecting the largest or smallest value.
answer_move: Build a candidates table: endpoints plus interior critical points, then compare f-values.
common_point_loss: Comparing derivative values instead of function values or omitting endpoints.

title: Determining Concavity
what_it_is: Concavity describes whether slopes are increasing or decreasing and is determined by the sign of the second derivative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding where f'' is positive or negative and translating that sign into concave up or concave down intervals.
answer_move: Make a sign chart for f'' and state concavity on intervals.
common_point_loss: Using f' sign to decide concavity instead of f'' sign.

title: Using the Second Derivative Test
what_it_is: The second derivative test can classify certain critical points using the sign of f'' at the point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by confirming f'(c)=0 or undefined as needed and then using f''(c) to classify the local behavior when possible.
answer_move: Check the critical point first, then use f''(c)>0 for local minimum or f''(c)<0 for local maximum.
common_point_loss: Using the test when f''(c)=0 and treating an inconclusive result as a conclusion.

title: Sketching Graphs of Functions and Their Derivatives
what_it_is: Graph sketching connects function values, derivative signs, slope behavior, extrema, and concavity into one representation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using derivative evidence to place increasing/decreasing intervals, extrema, concavity, and inflection behavior correctly.
answer_move: Annotate the derivative evidence first, then sketch only what the evidence supports.
common_point_loss: Drawing a graph from intuition without tying features to derivative sign or second-derivative sign.

title: Connecting a Function, Its First Derivative, and Its Second Derivative
what_it_is: This topic asks students to translate among f, f', and f'' in graphs, tables, and symbolic forms.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting f' to slope and f'' to change in slope, then using those links to justify behavior.
answer_move: Ask which graph or table represents values, slopes, or changes in slopes before answering.
common_point_loss: Confusing the graph of f with the graph of f' when identifying extrema or concavity.

title: Introduction to Optimization Problems
what_it_is: Optimization uses derivatives to find maximum or minimum values of a quantity under given constraints.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the quantity to optimize, writing it as a one-variable function, and identifying the relevant domain.
answer_move: Define variables, write the objective function, use the constraint to reduce to one variable, then state the domain.
common_point_loss: Differentiating before creating a valid one-variable objective function.

title: Solving Optimization Problems
what_it_is: Solving optimization problems means finding candidates, testing them, and interpreting the best value in context.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the objective, finding critical points in the domain, justifying max or min, and answering the contextual question.
answer_move: After setup, solve f'(x)=0, test candidates, then answer with units and the requested variable.
common_point_loss: Finding a critical point but not proving it gives the requested maximum or minimum.

title: Exploring Behaviors of Implicit Relations
what_it_is: Implicit relations can have slopes, extrema, and concavity even when they are not written as y = f(x).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using implicit differentiation to obtain dy/dx and then applying behavior rules to the relation.
answer_move: Differentiate implicitly, solve for dy/dx, then evaluate slope or behavior at the specified point.
common_point_loss: Trying to treat y as a constant or assuming the relation is already solved for y.

title: Exploring Accumulations of Change
what_it_is: Accumulation describes how small changes add up over an interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by interpreting a rate over an interval as accumulated change and connecting area under a rate graph to total amount.
answer_move: Identify the rate, identify the interval, then describe the accumulation as total change over that interval.
common_point_loss: Treating the rate value at one point as the accumulated total over an interval.

title: Approximating Areas with Riemann Sums
what_it_is: Riemann sums approximate accumulated area using rectangles based on left, right, midpoint, or other sample values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the correct subinterval widths and sample heights, then summing width times height with units.
answer_move: For each subinterval, compute base times chosen height, then add the products.
common_point_loss: Using the wrong endpoint or assuming all subintervals have equal width when they do not.

title: Riemann Sums, Summation Notation, and Definite Integral Notation
what_it_is: This topic connects rectangle sums, sigma notation, and definite integrals as representations of accumulated change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching limits of integration, subinterval structure, and integrand meaning to the accumulation being represented.
answer_move: Translate the notation into total accumulation from a to b of the rate or height function.
common_point_loss: Misreading the bounds or treating definite integral notation as an antiderivative request only.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Accumulation Functions
what_it_is: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links accumulation functions to derivatives of their integrands.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing that the derivative of an accumulation function depends on the integrand and any variable bound behavior.
answer_move: For F(x)=integral from a to x of f(t)dt, write F'(x)=f(x); adjust with chain rule if the bound is not x.
common_point_loss: Replacing the accumulation function with a number or forgetting the chain rule for variable bounds.

title: Interpreting the Behavior of Accumulation Functions
what_it_is: Accumulation functions increase or decrease based on the sign of the rate being accumulated, and their concavity depends on how that rate changes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting the integrand to the derivative of the accumulation function and then reasoning about sign or slope.
answer_move: Treat the integrand as F'(x), then use derivative-sign logic to discuss F.
common_point_loss: Judging the accumulation function directly from the area picture without using the integrand as its derivative.

title: Applying Properties of Definite Integrals
what_it_is: Definite integral properties allow students to split, combine, reverse, and scale accumulated quantities.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying interval additivity, sign reversal, constant multiples, and symmetry when appropriate.
answer_move: Rewrite the requested integral in terms of known intervals or areas before calculating.
common_point_loss: Adding areas without accounting for sign or reversed bounds.

title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Definite Integrals
what_it_is: The evaluation part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus uses antiderivatives to compute exact definite integrals.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding a valid antiderivative, evaluating it at the bounds, and subtracting upper minus lower.
answer_move: Find F, then compute F(b)-F(a) and attach contextual units when the integral represents change.
common_point_loss: Subtracting in the wrong order or forgetting that a definite integral can be negative when it represents signed change.

title: Finding Antiderivatives and Indefinite Integrals
what_it_is: An antiderivative reverses differentiation, and an indefinite integral represents a family of functions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using correct reverse derivative rules and including +C for indefinite integrals.
answer_move: Ask what function would differentiate to this expression, then include the constant of integration when no bounds are present.
common_point_loss: Forgetting +C or applying derivative rules forward instead of reversing them.

title: Integrating Using Substitution
what_it_is: Substitution reverses the chain rule by changing variables so a composite integrand becomes simpler.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing u, computing du, rewriting the integral consistently, and adjusting bounds for definite integrals when used.
answer_move: Choose the inside expression as u, find du, rewrite everything in u, then integrate.
common_point_loss: Leaving a mix of x and u in the same integral or forgetting to adjust definite bounds.

title: Integrating Functions Using Long Division and Completing the Square
what_it_is: Some rational expressions must be rewritten by long division or completing the square before integration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by rewriting the integrand into an equivalent form and then applying the appropriate antiderivative rule.
answer_move: When the integral does not match a basic form, rewrite the algebra first, then integrate the simpler pieces.
common_point_loss: Trying to integrate a complicated rational expression directly without making the needed algebraic rewrite.

title: Integrating Using Integration by Parts
what_it_is: Integration by parts rewrites an integral of a product using a derivative-antiderivative tradeoff.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing u and dv, computing du and v, and applying integral u dv = uv - integral v du accurately.
answer_move: Pick u to simplify when differentiated and dv to integrate cleanly, then write the full by-parts formula.
common_point_loss: Dropping the remaining integral or reversing signs in the uv - integral v du step.

title: Integrating Using Linear Partial Fractions
what_it_is: Linear partial fraction decomposition rewrites a rational function with distinct linear denominator factors as a sum of simpler fractions, each with one linear factor, before integrating.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by factoring the denominator into distinct linear factors, setting up the decomposition explicitly, solving for each constant, and integrating each resulting term to a logarithm.
answer_move: Factor the denominator into distinct linear factors, write A/(x-a) + B/(x-b), solve for A and B, then integrate each simpler fraction separately.
common_point_loss: Attempting the technique on a repeated linear factor or an irreducible quadratic factor, both of which are out of scope for this exam.

title: Evaluating Improper Integrals
what_it_is: An improper integral has an infinite bound or a discontinuous integrand, and is evaluated as the limit of a proper definite integral as the problematic bound is approached.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by rewriting the improper integral explicitly as a limit, evaluating that limit, and stating convergence to a finite value or divergence based on the actual result.
answer_move: Rewrite the improper integral as a limit of a proper integral, evaluate the limit, then state convergence or divergence based on whether the limit is a finite number.
common_point_loss: Substituting infinity directly into an antiderivative instead of taking an explicit limit, or not splitting an interior discontinuity into two separate improper integrals.

title: Selecting Techniques for Antidifferentiation
what_it_is: This topic is about choosing a valid integration method based on the structure of the integrand.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching the integrand structure to an antidifferentiation procedure before calculating.
answer_move: Classify the integrand first: basic reverse rule, composite needing substitution, rational needing rewrite, or product needing another technique.
common_point_loss: Forcing substitution or a memorized pattern when the integrand structure points elsewhere.

title: Modeling Situations with Differential Equations
what_it_is: Differential equations model situations where a quantity's rate of change depends on variables in the situation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by translating verbal rate relationships into equations involving dy/dx or related notation.
answer_move: Identify the quantity, identify what controls its rate, then write the differential equation with the correct variables.
common_point_loss: Writing a formula for y instead of an equation for the rate of change.

title: Verifying Solutions for Differential Equations
what_it_is: A proposed solution satisfies a differential equation if its derivative matches the rate expression after substitution.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the proposed solution and comparing it to the right-hand side of the differential equation.
answer_move: Compute dy/dx from the proposed y, substitute y and x into the differential equation, then show they match.
common_point_loss: Checking only the initial condition or only the equation, rather than verifying both when both are asked.

title: Sketching Slope Fields
what_it_is: A slope field shows small line segments whose slopes come from a differential equation at points in the plane.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by computing slopes at specified points and drawing segments with correct relative direction and steepness.
answer_move: Plug each point into dy/dx, then draw a short segment with that slope at the point.
common_point_loss: Drawing solution curves when the task asks for field segments, or ignoring the sign of the slope.

title: Reasoning Using Slope Fields
what_it_is: Slope fields allow students to infer solution behavior, equilibrium behavior, and approximate paths from local slopes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting the displayed segment slopes to whether solutions increase, decrease, level off, or change direction.
answer_move: Follow the local directions of the field and describe the solution curve consistent with nearby slopes.
common_point_loss: Reading the slope field as a graph of y-values rather than as directions for solution curves.

title: Approximating Solutions Using Euler's Method
what_it_is: Euler's Method uses repeated tangent-line steps to approximate a solution to a differential equation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the current point to compute slope, multiplying by step size, and updating y at each step.
answer_move: Make a row for each step: x, y, slope, delta y, new y.
common_point_loss: Using the slope from the endpoint instead of the current point or skipping intermediate steps.

title: Finding General Solutions Using Separation of Variables
what_it_is: Separation of variables solves certain differential equations by placing y terms with dy and x terms with dx before integrating.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating variables correctly, integrating both sides, and including the constant of integration.
answer_move: Move all y terms to one side and x terms to the other, integrate, then include +C.
common_point_loss: Mixing x and y after separation or omitting the integration constant.

title: Finding Particular Solutions Using Initial Conditions and Separation of Variables
what_it_is: A particular solution uses an initial condition to determine the constant in a general differential equation solution.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by solving generally, substituting the initial condition, determining C, and presenting the particular solution.
answer_move: Do not wait until the end mentally: substitute the given point clearly to solve for C.
common_point_loss: Leaving the answer with an undetermined C or applying the initial condition to the derivative instead of the solution.

title: Exponential Models with Differential Equations
what_it_is: Exponential models arise when a quantity changes at a rate proportional to the quantity itself.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing dy/dt = ky structure and interpreting the sign and meaning of k in context.
answer_move: Look for rate proportional to amount, then write or use the exponential solution model with the initial value.
common_point_loss: Using a linear model when the rate depends on the current amount.

title: Logistic Models with Differential Equations
what_it_is: Logistic models describe growth that slows as a population approaches a carrying capacity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying carrying capacity, growth intervals, and how the rate changes with population size.
answer_move: Use the factors in the differential equation to find equilibria and describe behavior relative to carrying capacity.
common_point_loss: Treating logistic growth as ordinary exponential growth with no upper limit.

title: Finding the Average Value of a Function on an Interval
what_it_is: Average value uses a definite integral divided by interval length to find the function's mean height over an interval.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by setting up 1/(b-a) times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx and interpreting the result with correct units.
answer_move: Write the formula before evaluating so the interval length and integral are both visible.
common_point_loss: Confusing average value with slope between endpoints.

title: Connecting Position, Velocity, and Acceleration Using Integrals
what_it_is: Integrals connect velocity to change in position and acceleration to change in velocity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using definite integrals to compute displacement or change in velocity and by distinguishing displacement from distance traveled.
answer_move: Identify whether the integral of velocity gives displacement or whether total distance requires integrating speed.
common_point_loss: Reporting displacement when the question asks for total distance traveled.

title: Using Accumulation Functions and Definite Integrals in Applied Contexts
what_it_is: Definite integrals in context accumulate rates into total change for quantities like volume, population, temperature, or cost.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the rate, integrating over the correct interval, and adding an initial value when the question asks for an amount.
answer_move: Use final amount = initial amount + accumulated change when an initial value is given.
common_point_loss: Forgetting the initial amount or attaching the rate's units instead of the accumulated quantity's units.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves Expressed as Functions of x
what_it_is: Area between x-functions uses vertical slices and integrates top function minus bottom function.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding intersection bounds and integrating upper minus lower over each interval.
answer_move: Sketch or compare functions to identify top and bottom, then integrate top minus bottom with respect to x.
common_point_loss: Reversing top and bottom or failing to split intervals when the top function changes.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves Expressed as Functions of y
what_it_is: Area between y-functions uses horizontal slices and integrates right function minus left function with respect to y.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using y-bounds and subtracting left from right in the horizontal-slice setup.
answer_move: Identify rightmost x and leftmost x as functions of y, then integrate right minus left dy.
common_point_loss: Using dx bounds or top-minus-bottom logic when the setup requires horizontal slices.

title: Finding the Area Between Curves That Intersect at More Than Two Points
what_it_is: When curves intersect more than twice, the region may need to be split into intervals with different top-bottom relationships.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying all relevant intersection points, splitting the region, and using the correct subtraction order on each interval.
answer_move: Find every intersection, draw or test each interval, then add the separate area integrals.
common_point_loss: Using one integral across the whole interval when the upper and lower functions switch.

title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Squares and Rectangles
what_it_is: Cross-section volume sums areas of slices whose square or rectangular dimensions are based on a region in the base.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the slice width, writing the cross-sectional area formula, and integrating that area over the correct bounds.
answer_move: Base of slice from the region first, area formula second, integral of area last.
common_point_loss: Integrating a length instead of an area or using the wrong side length for the cross section.

title: Volumes with Cross Sections: Triangles and Semicircles
what_it_is: Triangular and semicircular cross sections use geometry formulas to turn base lengths into slice areas.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the cross-section shape, substituting the region's base length into the correct area formula, and integrating.
answer_move: Write the shape formula before substituting the base length from the graph or equations.
common_point_loss: Using square cross-section area when the problem specifies triangles or semicircles.

title: Volume with Disc Method: Revolving Around the x- or y-Axis
what_it_is: The disc method finds volume by integrating circular cross-sectional areas when a region rotates around a coordinate axis without a hole.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the radius perpendicular to the axis of rotation and integrating pi times radius squared over the correct bounds.
answer_move: Draw the radius from the axis to the curve, then write pi r^2 for the slice area.
common_point_loss: Using diameter as radius or choosing a radius parallel to the axis of rotation.

title: Volume with Disc Method: Revolving Around Other Axes
what_it_is: Disc method around a non-coordinate axis still uses circular slices, but the radius is a distance to the given line of rotation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by expressing the radius as the distance from the curve to the rotation axis and integrating pi r^2.
answer_move: Write radius = distance to axis, then square it inside pi r^2.
common_point_loss: Using f(x) as the radius when the axis is shifted away from the coordinate axis.

title: Volume with Washer Method: Revolving Around the x- or y-Axis
what_it_is: The washer method finds volume when rotation creates an outer radius and an inner radius.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying both radii and integrating pi times outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
answer_move: Draw both distances from the axis, label outer and inner, then write pi(R^2-r^2).
common_point_loss: Subtracting radii before squaring or reversing inner and outer radii.

title: Volume with Washer Method: Revolving Around Other Axes
what_it_is: Washer method around a shifted axis uses outer and inner radii measured as distances to that axis.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining both shifted-axis distances and preserving the pi(R^2-r^2) structure.
answer_move: Measure each radius from the rotation line, not from the coordinate axis, then subtract areas.
common_point_loss: Forgetting to adjust radii for the shifted axis.

title: Arc Length of a Smooth Planar Curve
what_it_is: Arc length uses an integral built from the derivative to measure the length of a smooth curve.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by setting up the arc length integral with sqrt(1+(dy/dx)^2) over the correct interval.
answer_move: Find the derivative, square it inside the square-root expression, then integrate over the stated bounds.
common_point_loss: Using area under the curve instead of the arc length formula.

title: Defining and Differentiating Parametric Equations
what_it_is: Parametric equations define x and y as functions of a parameter, and dy/dx is found as (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) when dx/dt is not zero.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating each component with respect to the parameter, forming (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and checking dx/dt is not zero at the parameter value.
answer_move: Differentiate x(t) and y(t) separately first; then divide dy/dt by dx/dt only after confirming the denominator is nonzero.
common_point_loss: Treating dy/dx as dy/dt or dividing in the wrong order.

title: Second Derivatives of Parametric Equations
what_it_is: The second derivative for a parametric curve differentiates dy/dx with respect to the parameter and then divides by dx/dt.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by first finding dy/dx as a function of t, differentiating that expression with respect to t, and dividing by dx/dt.
answer_move: After finding dy/dx(t), compute d/dt of that expression, then divide by dx/dt.
common_point_loss: Differentiating dy/dx with respect to t and stopping before the second division by dx/dt.

title: Arc Lengths of Parametric Curves
what_it_is: The length of a parametrically defined curve is found with a definite integral built from the rates of change of x and y with respect to the parameter.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the parameter interval, differentiating both components, and building a positive length accumulation from both component rates.
answer_move: Find dx/dt and dy/dt, combine their rates into the arc-length integrand, and integrate over the parameter interval.
common_point_loss: Using only one component rate or integrating displacement instead of path length.

title: Defining and Differentiating Vector-Valued Functions
what_it_is: A vector-valued function outputs a vector, and differentiation extends real-valued derivative methods to each component.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by differentiating the component functions consistently and interpreting the derivative vector as the rate of change of the vector output.
answer_move: Differentiate each component with respect to the parameter and keep the result in vector form.
common_point_loss: Differentiating only one component or turning a vector derivative into a scalar without being asked.

title: Integrating Vector-Valued Functions
what_it_is: Integrating a vector-valued function extends integration methods to vector components, often producing displacement from a velocity vector.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by integrating each component over the interval and interpreting the resulting vector as net change when the integrand is velocity.
answer_move: Integrate component by component, then interpret the vector result as displacement or accumulated vector change.
common_point_loss: Calling the integral of velocity total distance instead of displacement.

title: Motion Problems Using Parametric and Vector-Valued Functions
what_it_is: Parametric and vector-valued motion problems use position, velocity, acceleration, speed, displacement, and distance in component form.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the requested quantity, using derivatives for velocity/acceleration, and using the correct integral for displacement or total distance.
answer_move: Name the quantity first: position, velocity, acceleration, displacement, speed, or distance; then choose derivative, vector integral, or speed integral accordingly.
common_point_loss: Using displacement when the question asks for total distance traveled, or vice versa.

title: Defining Polar Coordinates and Differentiating in Polar Form
what_it_is: A polar curve gives radius r as a function of theta, and derivatives of r, x, and y with respect to theta help analyze the curve.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using r(theta), x(theta)=r(theta)cos(theta), and y(theta)=r(theta)sin(theta) when needed, then applying derivative information to the curve.
answer_move: Translate polar to x and y when the question asks for rectangular position or horizontal/vertical behavior.
common_point_loss: Using r alone as x, or forgetting the cosine factor in x(theta).

title: Area of a Polar Region or the Area Bounded by a Single Polar Curve
what_it_is: Polar area is found with a definite integral over theta that accumulates sector-like area swept by a polar curve.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the correct theta bounds, using the polar area structure with r as a function of theta, and evaluating with the required constant included.
answer_move: Find the interval that traces the region once, set up the polar area integral with the correct constant, and evaluate carefully.
common_point_loss: Omitting the one-half constant or using bounds that trace the region more than once.

title: Area of the Region Bounded by Two Polar Curves
what_it_is: The area between two polar curves uses outer radius squared minus inner radius squared over the theta interval where the region is traced.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by solving for intersection angles, identifying which radius is outer on each interval, and integrating the polar area difference with the correct constant.
answer_move: Find theta bounds from intersections, test which curve is outside, and integrate one-half times outer squared minus inner squared.
common_point_loss: Subtracting radii instead of squared radii, or failing to split when outer and inner switch.

title: Defining Convergent and Divergent Infinite Series
what_it_is: An infinite series adds infinitely many terms, and convergence means its sequence of partial sums approaches a finite value.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by describing convergence in terms of partial sums and by recognizing that terms going to zero is necessary but not sufficient for series convergence.
answer_move: Ask what the partial sums do, not just what the individual terms do.
common_point_loss: Saying a series converges just because its terms approach zero.

title: Working with Geometric Series
what_it_is: A geometric series has a constant ratio, and sum ar^n converges to a/(1-r) when absolute value of r is less than 1.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying a and r, checking |r|<1, and using a/(1-r) only when the convergence condition is met.
answer_move: Find the common ratio first; if |r|<1, use a/(1-r). If not, state that the infinite series diverges.
common_point_loss: Using the sum formula when |r| is greater than or equal to 1.

title: The nth-Term Test for Divergence
what_it_is: The nth-term test shows divergence when the terms of a series do not approach zero.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding the limit of the terms and using a nonzero or nonexistent limit to conclude divergence only.
answer_move: Compute the term limit first; if it is not zero or does not exist, conclude the series diverges.
common_point_loss: Concluding convergence from a zero term limit.

title: Integral Test for Convergence
what_it_is: The integral test compares a positive decreasing series to an improper integral with matching function behavior.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking the test conditions, setting up the matching improper integral, and matching convergence or divergence conclusions.
answer_move: Confirm positive and decreasing behavior before using the improper integral.
common_point_loss: Using the integral test without checking that the function is positive and decreasing.

title: Harmonic Series and p-Series
what_it_is: The harmonic series diverges, while p-series converge for p>1 and diverge for p<=1.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by recognizing harmonic and p-series forms and using the correct p threshold.
answer_move: Rewrite the term to identify p, then compare p with 1 before concluding.
common_point_loss: Calling every constant multiple or shifted harmonic-like series exactly the harmonic series instead of comparing it appropriately.

title: Comparison Tests for Convergence
what_it_is: Comparison and limit comparison tests use known positive-term benchmark series to decide convergence or divergence.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing an appropriate positive benchmark and using comparison direction correctly for convergence or divergence.
answer_move: First confirm positive terms; then choose a benchmark with known behavior and compare in the direction that supports the conclusion.
common_point_loss: Using a comparison test directly on an alternating or mixed-sign series.

title: Alternating Series Test for Convergence
what_it_is: The alternating series test can prove convergence when alternating terms decrease in magnitude to zero.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by verifying alternation, decreasing magnitudes, and limit zero before concluding convergence.
answer_move: Check the sign pattern, the decreasing absolute values, and the zero limit in that order.
common_point_loss: Using the alternating series test when magnitudes do not decrease to zero.

title: Ratio Test for Convergence
what_it_is: The ratio test studies the limit of |a_{n+1}/a_n| and is one of the six convergence tests assessed for BC.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by setting up the ratio limit, interpreting less than 1 as absolute convergence and greater than 1 as divergence, and using another test when the limit equals 1.
answer_move: Form |a_{n+1}/a_n|, take the limit, and interpret the result against 1.
common_point_loss: Using the root test or treating ratio limit 1 as convergence.

title: Absolute and Conditional Convergence
what_it_is: A series converges absolutely if the series of absolute values converges; it converges conditionally if the original converges but the absolute-value series diverges.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by testing absolute convergence first when appropriate, then distinguishing absolute from conditional convergence with both required conclusions.
answer_move: Test the absolute-value series, then test the original series if the absolute-value series diverges.
common_point_loss: Claiming conditional convergence without showing the original converges and the absolute-value series diverges.

title: Alternating Series Error Bound
what_it_is: The alternating series error bound uses the first omitted term to bound the error of an alternating-series partial sum.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the first omitted term and stating the error is at most its magnitude.
answer_move: After choosing the partial sum, find the next term not included and use its absolute value as the error bound.
common_point_loss: Using the last included term instead of the first omitted term.

title: Taylor Polynomial Approximations of Functions
what_it_is: A Taylor polynomial uses derivatives at a center to approximate a function near that center.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct center, derivative values, factorial denominators, and powers of x-a.
answer_move: Build terms from f^(n)(a)/n! times (x-a)^n, keeping the center visible.
common_point_loss: Using powers of x when the polynomial is centered at a nonzero a.

title: Lagrange Error Bound
what_it_is: The Lagrange error bound gives a maximum possible Taylor-polynomial error using a bound on the next derivative.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct next derivative, factorial, distance from center, and by stating the error is at most the computed bound.
answer_move: Identify the next derivative and maximum bound M, compute M/(n+1)! times |x-a|^(n+1), then state an inequality.
common_point_loss: Saying the error equals the bound instead of is at most the bound.

title: Radius and Interval of Convergence of Power Series
what_it_is: A power series converges on an interval centered at its center, with a radius found first and endpoints tested separately.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding the radius, translating it into the open interval, testing both endpoints, and stating the final interval precisely.
answer_move: Find the center and radius, write the open interval, then test each endpoint with an assessed convergence test.
common_point_loss: Reporting only the radius or open interval without endpoint analysis.

title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series for a Function
what_it_is: A Taylor series represents a function with infinitely many Taylor terms; a Maclaurin series is a Taylor series centered at 0.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct base series, center, signs, powers, and factorial pattern when constructing a function series.
answer_move: Start from a known foundational series, then substitute, multiply, differentiate, or integrate term by term as allowed.
common_point_loss: Misremembering the signs or factorials in the foundational Maclaurin series.

title: Representing Functions as Power Series
what_it_is: Functions can be represented as power series by transforming known series, especially geometric and Maclaurin series.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by starting from a valid known series, performing legal algebraic or calculus transformations, and carrying the convergence interval through the transformation.
answer_move: Identify the parent series first, transform the function to match it, then update the interval or radius of convergence.
common_point_loss: Finding a correct series expression but omitting the interval of convergence.

title: Moles and Molar Mass
what_it_is: You cannot count individual atoms or molecules directly in the lab. The mole and Avogadro's number (6.022 x 10^23 per mol) give a bridge from a measurable mass to a particle count, using n = m/M.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by correctly using n = m/M (and its rearrangements) to convert between mass, moles, and particle count, and by using the right molar mass for the substance in question.
answer_move: Before calculating, write down what you are given (mass, moles, or particle count) and what you need, then choose n = m/M or n times Avogadro's number to connect them.
common_point_loss: Using the wrong molar mass, such as an element's molar mass in a compound problem, or miscounting atoms when summing a compound's molar mass from its formula.

title: Mass Spectra of Elements
what_it_is: A mass spectrum of a single element shows a peak for each isotope, positioned at that isotope's mass and sized by its relative abundance in a natural sample. Average atomic mass is the isotope-weighted average of those peaks.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading isotope mass and relative abundance off the spectrum, multiplying each isotope's mass by its fractional abundance, and summing to calculate the weighted average atomic mass.
answer_move: For each peak, multiply the isotope mass by its fractional abundance, then add the products across every peak to get the weighted average atomic mass.
common_point_loss: Attributing isotope mass differences to electrons or protons instead of neutrons.

title: Elemental Composition of Pure Substances
what_it_is: The law of definite proportions says the mass ratio of elements in any pure sample of a compound is always the same. The empirical formula is the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms that matches that mass ratio.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by converting given masses or mass percentages to moles of each element, dividing every mole value by the smallest one, and rounding to a whole-number ratio to get the empirical formula, then scaling to the molecular formula if molar mass is given.
answer_move: Assume a 100 g sample so mass percent becomes grams, convert each element's grams to moles, divide every mole value by the smallest mole value, then scale to whole numbers.
common_point_loss: Stopping at the empirical formula when the molecular formula was asked for, by not scaling the empirical formula using the ratio of given molar mass to empirical formula mass.

title: Composition of Mixtures
what_it_is: A pure substance contains one type of particle in a fixed proportion. A mixture contains two or more particle types whose proportions can vary from sample to sample. Elemental analysis can be used to check a sample's purity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using elemental analysis data across multiple samples to test whether a component ratio stays constant, and by using that evidence to argue whether a sample is a pure substance or a mixture.
answer_move: Compare the calculated mass ratio of components across two or more samples of the same material. A constant ratio supports a pure substance; a changing ratio supports a mixture.
common_point_loss: Assuming a sample is a pure substance just because it looks uniform or homogeneous, instead of checking whether its elemental composition ratio stays constant across independent samples.

title: Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration
what_it_is: An atom is a positively charged nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons. Coulomb's law describes the force between charged particles as proportional to q1 times q2 divided by r squared. Electron configuration follows the Aufbau principle, filling shells and subshells in order of increasing energy.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing correct ground-state electron configurations using the Aufbau filling order, and by using Coulomb's law reasoning, meaning charge and distance from the nucleus, to explain why a configuration produces a given property instead of only stating the property.
answer_move: Fill subshells in order of increasing energy (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, and so on), then explain any related property, such as ionization energy, using nuclear charge and electron distance or shielding rather than stopping at the configuration itself.
common_point_loss: Writing a correct electron configuration but then explaining a related property, such as ionization energy, with a vague label like periodic trend instead of grounding the explanation in nuclear charge and electron distance or shielding, which is what the Coulomb's law reasoning actually requires.

title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
what_it_is: In a photoelectron spectrum (PES), each peak's position shows the energy needed to remove an electron from a specific subshell, and each peak's height is approximately proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching a spectrum's peak positions and relative heights to a specific element's electron configuration, and by explaining that core electrons need more energy to remove because they are closer to the nucleus and less shielded than valence electrons.
answer_move: Count the number of peaks and compare their relative heights first to identify subshell electron counts, then match that pattern to a specific element's electron configuration before discussing binding energy.
common_point_loss: Confusing binding energy order with orbital filling order; a subshell with higher binding energy is held more tightly and closer to the nucleus, which is not necessarily the last subshell filled by the Aufbau principle.

title: Periodic Trends
what_it_is: Periodic table position reflects recurring electron configuration patterns. Trends in ionization energy, atomic and ionic radius, electron affinity, and electronegativity are explained qualitatively using Coulomb's law, shielding, and effective nuclear charge.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining a trend using effective nuclear charge and distance from the nucleus or shielding, not just by naming the trend's direction, and by using the trend to make a specific comparison or estimate when exact data is missing.
answer_move: For a trend question, choose whichever Coulombic factor actually differs between the two atoms or ions being compared, effective nuclear charge, distance from the nucleus, or shielding, and use only that factor to justify the direction of the trend.
common_point_loss: Correctly stating the direction of a trend, such as ionization energy increases across a period, without explaining why through effective nuclear charge and shielding; an unsupported direction claim does not earn the explanation point.

title: Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds
what_it_is: Bond formation is governed by how valence electrons interact with the nucleus. Elements in the same column tend to form analogous compounds, and an element's typical ionic charge can be predicted from its valence electron count and periodic table position.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by predicting an ion's typical charge from its group number or valence electron count, and by using that charge to predict a compound's formula or to identify an analogous compound for a same-column element.
answer_move: For common main-group ions, count valence electrons from the group number, determine how many electrons must be gained or lost to reach a noble-gas configuration, and use that number as the ion's typical charge.
common_point_loss: Guessing or misremembering an ionic charge instead of deriving it from valence electron count and group position, or proposing a compound formula whose total positive and negative charge does not balance to zero.

title: Types of Chemical Bonds
what_it_is: Bonding is a continuum set by how unequally two atoms pull on shared electrons. Electronegativity rises left-to-right across a period and falls down a group (shell model plus Coulomb's law). Similar electronegativities give nonpolar covalent bonds, unequal ones give polar covalent bonds with a bond dipole, and large differences give bonds we call ionic. Metals instead delocalize their valence electrons across the whole solid rather than assigning them to individual atoms.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from classifying a bond as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic AND justifying the classification with a stated electronegativity comparison, then using observed properties (conductivity when molten or dissolved, melting point, solubility, brittleness versus malleability) as the confirming evidence. Comparison items award credit for ranking bond polarity by relative electronegativity difference and for identifying which atom carries the partial negative charge.
answer_move: State the electronegativity comparison explicitly before naming the bond type ('O is more electronegative than H, so the shared electrons are pulled toward O -- polar covalent, with delta-negative on O'), and when the item gives you experimental properties, let those properties decide the classification rather than the metal/nonmetal shortcut.
common_point_loss: Treating ionic and covalent as two separate boxes, instead of a continuum where every polar bond already has some ionic character.

title: Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy
what_it_is: A graph of potential energy versus internuclear distance describes a bond quantitatively: the lowest point on the curve is the equilibrium bond length, and the depth of that well is the bond energy needed to pull the atoms apart. Higher bond order (single to double to triple) pulls the minimum to a shorter distance and deepens the well. For ions, Coulomb's law says larger charges and smaller ionic radii both strengthen the attraction.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly reading equilibrium bond length and bond energy off a PE curve, from ranking bond length and bond energy by bond order in the same breath (shorter goes with stronger), and from applying Coulomb's law to ion pairs by citing BOTH factors -- the magnitude of the charges and the internuclear distance set by ionic radii -- to justify which interaction is stronger.
answer_move: When you rank two ionic compounds, name charge and ionic size in the same sentence and say which one dominates (for example MgO over NaCl because 2+/2- charges outweigh any size difference); when reading a PE curve, quote the x-value at the minimum as bond length and the well depth as bond energy rather than describing the curve's shape.
common_point_loss: Comparing only ion charges and ignoring ionic radius, or claiming a longer bond is somehow stronger.

title: Structure of Ionic Solids
what_it_is: In an ionic solid, cations and anions occupy a systematic, repeating three-dimensional array. That arrangement is not arbitrary: it is the packing that puts oppositely charged ions as close as possible while keeping like-charged ions apart, maximizing attraction and minimizing repulsion across the whole lattice.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from describing the lattice as an extended periodic array of alternating cations and anions and explaining a macroscopic property by that arrangement -- for instance, that many strong Coulombic attractions throughout the lattice require large energy to disrupt (high melting point), or that shifting a layer aligns like charges and causes the crystal to fracture (brittleness).
answer_move: Explain ionic properties by the alternating-array arrangement and the many attractions it creates, not by memorizing lattice names -- the AP Exam explicitly does not assess knowledge of specific crystal structures, so naming a structure type earns nothing and is not expected of you.
common_point_loss: Describing an ionic solid as separate molecules or discrete ion pairs, rather than one extended lattice of alternating charges.

title: Structure of Metals and Alloys
what_it_is: A metal is an array of positive metal ions immersed in a sea of delocalized valence electrons that belong to the solid as a whole. Alloys come in two structural flavors: interstitial alloys, where much smaller atoms (carbon in iron, giving steel) sit in the gaps of the host lattice, and substitutional alloys, where atoms of comparable radius (as in some brass) replace host atoms in lattice positions.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from invoking mobile delocalized electrons to explain conductivity and from invoking layers of ions sliding past one another (with the electron sea still holding them together) to explain malleability, and from classifying an alloy as interstitial or substitutional by explicitly comparing the atomic radii of the two elements involved.
answer_move: Classify an alloy by comparing atomic radii out loud -- significantly different radii means the small atoms fill interstices (interstitial), comparable radii means one atom replaces another in lattice sites (substitutional) -- and cite the radius comparison as your reason, not the identity of the metals.
common_point_loss: Saying metals conduct because they 'have free electrons' without stating those delocalized electrons are mobile throughout the whole solid.

title: Lewis Diagrams
what_it_is: A Lewis diagram is a bookkeeping drawing of where every valence electron in a molecule or ion sits. You build it by a fixed procedure: total the valence electrons (adjusting for overall charge), choose a central atom and arrange the others around it, connect them with single bonds, then distribute the remaining electrons as lone pairs to satisfy octets, converting lone pairs into multiple bonds when a central atom comes up short.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from producing a complete, correct diagram: the total valence-electron count matches the formula (including added electrons for anions and removed electrons for cations), every bonding pair and lone pair is shown, octets are satisfied where the procedure requires, and an ion's diagram is enclosed in brackets with the overall charge written outside.
answer_move: Write the valence-electron total as a number before you draw anything, then count the electrons in your finished picture and confirm the two match -- and for a polyatomic ion, adjust that total for the charge and put brackets with the charge around the final structure.
common_point_loss: Drawing only the bonds and forgetting lone pairs, or ignoring an ion's charge when totaling valence electrons.

title: Resonance and Formal Charge
what_it_is: Two refinements sit on top of a finished Lewis diagram. When several EQUIVALENT diagrams are possible, resonance says the real molecule is a single averaged structure -- bonds intermediate in length and strength -- not a molecule flipping between forms. When candidate diagrams are NONEQUIVALENT, the octet rule plus formal charge picks the best one: minimize formal charges overall and place any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. The Lewis model has real limits, especially for odd-electron species.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from drawing all equivalent resonance forms and stating that the actual structure is an average of them (with bond order and bond length between the extremes), and separately from computing formal charge -- valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the bonding electrons -- for the competing atoms and justifying your chosen structure by minimized formal charges and by negative formal charge sitting on the more electronegative atom.
answer_move: Decide first whether your candidate structures are equivalent or nonequivalent: equivalent ones call for drawing the resonance set and describing an averaged structure, while nonequivalent ones call for showing the actual formal-charge arithmetic on the contested atoms and naming which structure wins and why.
common_point_loss: Saying the molecule rapidly switches between resonance forms; it is one averaged structure, and the bonds are identical.

title: VSEPR and Hybridization
what_it_is: VSEPR takes a finished Lewis diagram and predicts three-dimensional shape by assuming regions of electron density around a central atom repel one another and spread as far apart as possible. From that arrangement you get the molecular geometry (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent, trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, octahedral, square pyramidal, square planar), approximate bond angles, relative bond lengths and energies, whether the molecule has a net dipole, and the hybridization label sp (180 degrees), sp2 (120 degrees), or sp3 (109.5 degrees). Sigma bonds form by head-on overlap and are stronger; pi bonds, present in multiple bonds, are weaker and block rotation, producing geometric isomers.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from counting regions of electron density around the central atom (each lone pair counts as one, and a double or triple bond counts as ONE region), then naming the molecular geometry based on atom positions only, giving the associated bond angle, and -- when asked -- assigning the hybridization label. Polarity points require combining bond dipoles with the geometry to argue whether they cancel.
answer_move: Count regions of electron density first and count each multiple bond as a single region, then answer exactly what was asked -- a geometry name if the question says geometry, an sp/sp2/sp3 label if it says hybridization. Note the scope limit: hybridization labels stop at sp3, so for a central atom with more than four electron pairs give only the shape, and never reach for d-orbital hybridization or molecular orbital theory, which the exam does not assess.
common_point_loss: Counting a C=O double bond as two regions and answering sp3; a double bond is one region, so that carbon is sp2.

title: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
what_it_is: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum is the Properties of Substances and Mixtures topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: match microwave, infrared, and UV-visible absorption to rotational, vibrational, and electronic transitions.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you match microwave, infrared, and UV-visible absorption to rotational, vibrational, and electronic transitions, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then match microwave, infrared, and UV-visible absorption to rotational, vibrational, and electronic transitions before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
