title: Properties of Photons
what_it_is: A photon carries a discrete amount of energy. When a species absorbs or emits a photon, its energy changes by exactly that photon energy, with wavelength, frequency, and energy connected by c = lambda nu and E = h nu.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by converting wavelength and frequency consistently, using E = h nu for photon energy, and explaining absorption or emission as an energy-level change of the species rather than as a vague light interaction.
answer_move: Before calculating, identify whether the prompt gives wavelength, frequency, or energy; convert units first, then chain c = lambda nu into E = h nu only as needed.
common_point_loss: Using wavelength directly in E = h nu, or forgetting that shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher photon energy.

title: Beer-Lambert Law
what_it_is: The Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance to concentration: A = epsilon b c. For a fixed wavelength and cuvette path length, absorbance is directly proportional to the absorbing species concentration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying epsilon, path length, and concentration in A = epsilon b c; using proportional reasoning when wavelength and path length are fixed; and interpreting larger absorbance as more absorbing species in the light path.
answer_move: First check whether epsilon and path length stay constant; if they do, compare concentrations by comparing absorbances before plugging numbers into the full equation.
common_point_loss: Treating absorbance as proportional to path length or concentration without checking which variable changed, or assuming the spectrophotometer wavelength is arbitrary.

title: Introduction for Reactions
what_it_is: Chemical reactions rearrange matter into new substances, while physical changes alter properties or form without changing composition.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing physical from chemical change, naming evidence for reaction, and explaining what particles or substances changed rather than just listing an observation.
answer_move: State whether composition changes; then use the observation as evidence instead of treating the observation as the definition.
common_point_loss: Calling every color, phase, or temperature change chemical without explaining whether new substances formed.

title: Net Ionic Equations
what_it_is: Molecular, complete ionic, and net ionic equations are balanced symbolic forms that represent the same process at different levels of detail.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by dissociating strong aqueous electrolytes correctly, canceling spectator ions, preserving phases, and checking that atoms and charge balance.
answer_move: Write the complete ionic equation first; then cancel only species that are unchanged on both sides with the same phase and charge.
common_point_loss: Canceling a species that changes phase, formula, or charge, or balancing atoms while leaving total charge unequal.

title: Representations of Reactions
what_it_is: Reaction equations can be translated into particulate diagrams that show how particles combine, separate, or remain spectators.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching coefficients to particle counts, keeping spectator ions visible or absent according to representation type, and showing products consistent with the balanced equation.
answer_move: Start from the balanced equation; then count particles in the same ratios before drawing or interpreting the particulate model.
common_point_loss: Drawing particles that match formulas but not the balanced coefficient ratios.

title: Physical and Chemical Changes
what_it_is: Physical changes usually change intermolecular interactions only, while chemical changes usually involve bond breaking and bond forming.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by naming the particle-level interaction that changes and explaining whether composition changes or only attractions between particles change.
answer_move: Identify what bonds or intermolecular forces are changing before labeling the process physical or chemical.
common_point_loss: Treating every separation of particles as chemical or every dissolution as automatically physical without particle-level reasoning.

title: Stoichiometry
what_it_is: Stoichiometry uses balanced-equation coefficients as mole ratios to calculate reactant or product amounts.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by converting given information to moles, using the balanced mole ratio, and converting to the requested units, including mass when mass comparison is asked.
answer_move: Use the balanced equation only after converting to moles; then convert back to the unit the prompt asks for.
common_point_loss: Stopping at a mole-ratio comparison when the question asks for a mass comparison.

title: Introduction to Titration
what_it_is: A titration uses a known-concentration titrant that reacts quantitatively with an analyte; equivalence point and endpoint are related but not identical.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the balanced reaction to relate titrant and analyte moles, distinguishing endpoint from equivalence point, and solving concentration from volume and molarity data.
answer_move: Find moles of titrant from M and V, use the balanced mole ratio at equivalence, then divide analyte moles by analyte volume.
common_point_loss: Assuming endpoint means exact equivalence without considering the indicator or observable signal.

title: Types of Chemical Reactions
what_it_is: Common reaction types include acid-base proton transfer, redox electron transfer, combustion, and precipitation from aqueous ions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying proton transfer, oxidation-number change, hydrocarbon combustion products, or insoluble product formation using the allowed solubility facts.
answer_move: Look for the reaction signature first: H+ transfer, oxidation-number change, CO2/H2O combustion products, or solid-forming ion exchange.
common_point_loss: Memorizing broad reaction labels without showing the particle or oxidation-number evidence that supports the label.

title: Introduction to Acid-Base Reactions
what_it_is: Bronsted-Lowry acids donate protons and Bronsted-Lowry bases accept protons in aqueous acid-base reactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the proton donor and acceptor, pairing each acid with its conjugate base, and reasoning from ionization when comparing relative strength.
answer_move: Track the transferred H+; the species that loses H+ is the acid and the species that gains H+ is the base.
common_point_loss: Calling a species an acid because it contains H without showing that it donates H+ in the reaction.

title: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
what_it_is: Redox reactions transfer electrons and can be balanced by separating oxidation and reduction half-reactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by assigning oxidation numbers, identifying oxidation and reduction, placing electrons on the correct side of half-reactions, and combining half-reactions to balance charge and atoms.
answer_move: Write the oxidation-number changes first; then place electrons as products for oxidation and reactants for reduction.
common_point_loss: Writing the reduction direction for a species being oxidized, or omitting electrons from the half-reaction.

title: Reaction Rates
what_it_is: Reaction rate measures how fast reactants are converted to products, usually through concentration change per unit time.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading slope or concentration change over time, using balanced-equation ratios to compare rates, and explaining how concentration, temperature, surface area, or catalysts affect rate.
answer_move: Identify which species is changing; then use the balanced coefficients to relate its rate to the reaction rate or another species rate.
common_point_loss: Comparing concentration slopes without adjusting for the balanced-equation coefficients.

title: Introduction to Rate Law
what_it_is: A rate law relates reaction rate to reactant concentrations raised to experimentally determined orders.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by comparing initial-rate trials, finding individual orders, adding orders for overall order, and giving rate-constant units that match the overall order.
answer_move: Compare trials where only one reactant concentration changes; then connect the rate factor to the concentration factor.
common_point_loss: Using balanced-equation coefficients as reaction orders for a non-elementary overall reaction.

title: Concentration Changes over Time
what_it_is: Integrated rate laws connect concentration to time, with linear graph tests distinguishing zero-, first-, and second-order reactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the graph that is linear, using the matching integrated rate law, reading k from slope sign and magnitude, and applying t_1/2 = 0.693/k only for first order.
answer_move: Test which plot is linear: [A] vs t, ln[A] vs t, or 1/[A] vs t; then use the matching equation.
common_point_loss: Using first-order half-life or ln[A] linearity for every reaction order.

title: Elementary Reactions
what_it_is: An elementary reaction is a single molecular event, so its rate law follows directly from the particles colliding in that step.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying molecularity, writing the elementary-step rate law from reactants in that step, and not applying that shortcut to an overall non-elementary equation.
answer_move: Ask whether the equation is one elementary step; only then use its reactant coefficients as rate-law powers.
common_point_loss: Writing a rate law from the overall balanced equation when the problem describes a multistep mechanism.

title: Collision Model
what_it_is: The collision model says reactions require particles to collide with enough energy and proper orientation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking rate changes to collision frequency, collision orientation, and the fraction of particles with energy at or above activation energy.
answer_move: Explain the rate change through successful collisions, not just more collisions.
common_point_loss: Saying higher temperature increases rate only because particles collide more often, without mentioning the larger fraction above activation energy.

title: Reaction Energy Profile
what_it_is: A reaction energy profile shows reactants, transition state, products, activation energy, and overall energy change along a reaction coordinate.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying forward and reverse activation energies, determining endothermic or exothermic character, and explaining rate-temperature effects qualitatively.
answer_move: Mark reactants, products, and the peak first; then measure activation energy from the reactants to the transition state.
common_point_loss: Confusing activation energy with overall enthalpy change between reactants and products.

title: Introduction to Reaction Mechanisms
what_it_is: A reaction mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that sum to the overall reaction, often containing intermediates and catalysts.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by summing elementary steps, canceling species correctly, distinguishing intermediates from catalysts, and checking that the mechanism matches the overall reaction.
answer_move: Add the elementary steps and cancel species that appear on both sides; then classify canceled species by when they are produced or consumed.
common_point_loss: Calling every canceled species a spectator ion instead of deciding whether it is an intermediate or catalyst in the mechanism.

title: Reaction Mechanism and Rate Law
what_it_is: For many mechanisms, the slow elementary step determines the overall rate law, especially when the first step is rate-limiting.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the slow step, writing its elementary rate law, and replacing intermediates only when the mechanism information requires it.
answer_move: Find the slow step first; then write the rate law from that elementary step rather than from the overall equation.
common_point_loss: Using the overall reaction coefficients instead of the slow elementary step to write the rate law.

title: Pre-Equilibrium Approximation
what_it_is: Pre-equilibrium reasoning is used when an early fast reversible step establishes an equilibrium before a later rate-limiting step.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing the slow-step rate law, using the fast pre-equilibrium relationship to express the intermediate in terms of reactants, and substituting cleanly.
answer_move: Write the slow-step rate law first; then use the earlier equilibrium expression only to replace the intermediate.
common_point_loss: Leaving an intermediate in the final rate law even though it is not a reactant in the overall reaction.

title: Multistep Reaction Energy Profile
what_it_is: A multistep energy profile shows separate activation barriers and intermediates for each elementary step in a mechanism.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching peaks to transition states, valleys to intermediates, comparing activation energies, and connecting the largest barrier to the rate-determining step.
answer_move: Count the peaks and valleys; then label each step barrier before deciding which step is slowest.
common_point_loss: Calling the final product valley an intermediate or using total energy change as the slow-step barrier.

title: Catalysis
what_it_is: A catalyst increases reaction rate by providing an alternate pathway, often lowering activation energy, and is regenerated by the end of the mechanism.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by citing the specific steps showing catalyst consumption and regeneration, distinguishing catalysts from intermediates, and connecting the alternate pathway to rate increase.
answer_move: Use the individual mechanism steps, not only the overall equation, to prove which species is the catalyst.
common_point_loss: Saying a species is a catalyst only because it lowers activation energy, without citing its consumption and regeneration in the mechanism.

title: Endothermic and Exothermic Processes
what_it_is: Endothermic processes absorb energy from surroundings; exothermic processes release energy to surroundings.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the system, tracking energy flow, connecting temperature change to surroundings, and assigning the correct sign for the process.
answer_move: Name the system first; then decide whether energy enters or leaves that system.
common_point_loss: Calling a process exothermic just because the system temperature is higher without identifying system and surroundings.

title: Energy Diagrams
what_it_is: Energy diagrams show whether products or final states are higher or lower in energy than reactants or initial states.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by labeling reactants and products, reading Delta H sign from vertical position, and distinguishing overall energy change from activation energy when relevant.
answer_move: Compare product energy to reactant energy before deciding endothermic or exothermic.
common_point_loss: Reading only the arrow direction and ignoring whether products are above or below reactants.

title: Heat Transfer and Thermal Equilibrium
what_it_is: Heat transfer is energy transfer from warmer particles to cooler particles through collisions until thermal equilibrium is reached.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by describing particle collision energy transfer, identifying warmer-to-cooler direction, and explaining equilibrium as equal average kinetic energy.
answer_move: Track average kinetic energy through collisions, then state when temperatures become equal.
common_point_loss: Saying thermal equilibrium means both objects contain the same total thermal energy.

title: Heat Capacity and Calorimetry
what_it_is: Calorimetry uses q = mc Delta T to connect heat transfer with mass, specific heat, and temperature change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the correct mass, specific heat, and Delta T; applying energy conservation; assigning system sign from observed temperature change; and reporting appropriate significant figures.
answer_move: Use total solution mass when appropriate, calculate q for the surroundings, then flip sign for the reacting system if needed.
common_point_loss: Using only solute mass in q=mc Delta T or dropping the negative sign for an exothermic reaction.

title: Energy of Phase Changes
what_it_is: Phase changes absorb or release energy while temperature stays constant for a pure substance during the change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying whether energy is absorbed or released, using phase-change enthalpy with the correct sign, and not changing temperature during the plateau.
answer_move: Decide whether the process moves to a more separated or less separated phase; then assign energy input or release.
common_point_loss: Using q=mc Delta T during a phase-change plateau where temperature is constant.

title: Introduction to Enthalpy of Reaction
what_it_is: Reaction enthalpy is the heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure, with negative Delta H for exothermic reactions and positive Delta H for endothermic reactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by connecting temperature change to reaction sign, scaling heat by moles reacted when needed, and distinguishing reaction-system energy from solution or surroundings energy.
answer_move: Use the observed temperature change to decide heat flow, then report Delta H for the reaction with the system sign.
common_point_loss: Reporting positive Delta H for a reaction that warms the solution without accounting for heat released by the reacting system.

title: Bond Enthalpies
what_it_is: Bond enthalpy estimates compare energy required to break reactant bonds with energy released when product bonds form.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by counting all broken and formed bonds, summing average bond energies, and using broken minus formed to estimate Delta H.
answer_move: List bonds broken and bonds formed separately before substituting numbers.
common_point_loss: Treating bond formation as energy absorbed or forgetting coefficient-based bond counts.

title: Enthalpy of Formation
what_it_is: Standard enthalpy of formation values combine as Delta H reaction = sum products minus sum reactants.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by multiplying each formation enthalpy by its coefficient, summing products and reactants separately, and subtracting reactants from products.
answer_move: Write products minus reactants and include coefficients before calculating.
common_point_loss: Reversing the subtraction or forgetting to multiply formation values by balanced coefficients.

title: Hess's Law
what_it_is: Hess law uses reaction addition: reversing, scaling, and summing equations changes Delta H in matching ways.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reversing equations when needed, multiplying equations and Delta H together, canceling species to match the target, and only then summing enthalpies.
answer_move: Make the equations sum to the target first; then add the adjusted Delta H values.
common_point_loss: Adding the listed Delta H values without checking whether the adjusted equations actually produce the target reaction.

title: Introduction to Equilibrium
what_it_is: Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates while macroscopic amounts stay constant.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by stating both equal rates and constant amounts, and by distinguishing dynamic equilibrium from reaction completion.
answer_move: Name the forward and reverse processes, then compare their rates rather than saying the reaction stopped.
common_point_loss: Saying equilibrium means all reaction has stopped.

title: Direction of Reversible Reactions
what_it_is: A reversible system moves in the net direction of the faster process until forward and reverse rates become equal.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by comparing forward and reverse rates and identifying when net change ceases.
answer_move: Ask which rate is larger now; the system shifts in that net direction until rates match.
common_point_loss: Choosing shift direction from the larger concentration side only.

title: Reaction Quotient and Equilibrium Constant
what_it_is: Q and K use the same expression form, but Q describes any moment and K describes equilibrium.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing the expression with correct powers, excluding solids and pure liquids, and comparing Q with K.
answer_move: Write the expression from gases or aqueous species only; then compare Q to K.
common_point_loss: Including a solid in Ksp or putting the coefficient on the wrong species.

title: Calculating the Equilibrium Constant
what_it_is: K can be calculated from measured equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures substituted into the correct expression.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by confirming the system is at equilibrium, substituting equilibrium values, and preserving powers from coefficients.
answer_move: Write the K expression first, then substitute equilibrium values only.
common_point_loss: Using initial concentrations as if they were equilibrium concentrations.

title: Magnitude of the Equilibrium Constant
what_it_is: A large K means products are favored at equilibrium; a small K means reactants are favored.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by interpreting K relative to 1 and separating extent from rate.
answer_move: Compare K to 1, then state whether products or reactants dominate at equilibrium.
common_point_loss: Saying a large K means the reaction happens quickly.

title: Properties of the Equilibrium Constant
what_it_is: Changing the written reaction changes K: reverse inverts K, scaling raises K to a power, and adding reactions multiplies K values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying the same equation manipulation to K before combining values.
answer_move: Manipulate the reaction first; then transform K to match that exact reaction.
common_point_loss: Adding K values when reactions are added.

title: Calculating Equilibrium Concentrations
what_it_is: Equilibrium concentrations can be predicted from initial amounts, balanced changes, and K.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by comparing Q to K, setting up changes with coefficients, and solving for equilibrium values.
answer_move: Use Q to decide shift direction, then build the change row from balanced coefficients.
common_point_loss: Changing every concentration by the same amount instead of coefficient-scaled amounts.

title: Representations of Equilibrium
what_it_is: Particulate diagrams can represent equilibrium by showing stable reactant and product particle ratios consistent with K.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by counting particles, connecting ratios to K magnitude, and showing ongoing reversible change if asked.
answer_move: Count reactant and product particles before interpreting which side is favored.
common_point_loss: Using a picture with equal amounts to represent every equilibrium.

title: Introduction to Le Chatelier's Principle
what_it_is: Le Chatelier reasoning predicts how an equilibrium system responds to a stress by opposing the disturbance.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the stress, predicting the shift, and stating the measurable result.
answer_move: Name the stress first; then state which direction consumes what was added or replaces what was removed.
common_point_loss: Treating every stress as changing K, including concentration changes.

title: Reaction Quotient and Le Chatelier's Principle
what_it_is: A stress takes Q away from K, and the system shifts until Q equals K again; temperature changes K itself.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by explaining whether Q or K changed and how the shift restores equality.
answer_move: After a stress, decide whether Q changed, K changed, or both; then predict how Q moves back toward K.
common_point_loss: Saying concentration changes alter K instead of Q.

title: Introduction to Solubility Equilibria
what_it_is: Ksp describes the equilibrium between a sparingly soluble ionic solid and its dissolved ions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing Ksp without the solid, using ion coefficients as powers, and connecting molar solubility to ion concentrations.
answer_move: Write the dissolution equation first; then build Ksp from dissolved ions only.
common_point_loss: Putting the solid in Ksp or forgetting to square an ion concentration from a coefficient of 2.

title: Common-Ion Effect
what_it_is: A common ion lowers solubility by shifting a dissolution equilibrium toward the solid.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the common ion, predicting the shift, and explaining whether solubility increases or decreases.
answer_move: Find the ion shared with the salt; then decide whether the equilibrium forms more solid or dissolves more solid.
common_point_loss: Memorizing a rule without explaining the ion-level shift.

title: Introduction to Acids and Bases
what_it_is: pH, pOH, Kw, and pKw connect hydronium and hydroxide concentrations in water.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using pH=-log[H3O+], pOH=-log[OH-], Kw, and pH+pOH=14 at 25 C only.
answer_move: Identify whether the prompt gives hydronium, hydroxide, pH, or pOH before converting.
common_point_loss: Assuming pH 7 is neutral at every temperature.

title: pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases
what_it_is: Strong acids fully ionize and strong bases fully dissociate, so initial concentration determines hydronium or hydroxide concentration.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying strong acid/base, accounting for hydroxide stoichiometry, and converting pOH to pH when needed.
answer_move: For strong bases, find [OH-] first, then convert pOH to pH if the prompt asks for pH.
common_point_loss: Reporting pOH as pH after a strong-base calculation.

title: Weak Acid and Base Equilibria
what_it_is: Weak acids and bases partially ionize, so Ka, Kb, pKa, pKb, and percent ionization describe equilibrium extent.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing the correct equilibrium expression, solving for equilibrium concentrations, and connecting stronger acid/base to larger Ka/Kb or smaller pKa/pKb.
answer_move: Write the acid or base ionization equation first; then build the equilibrium expression from products over reactants.
common_point_loss: Treating a weak acid as fully ionized just because an initial concentration is given.

title: Acid-Base Reactions and Buffers
what_it_is: Acid-base reactions are proton-transfer stoichiometry followed by pH reasoning from the species left after reaction.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by doing mole stoichiometry first, identifying excess or equimolar conditions, and choosing the correct pH method.
answer_move: React acid and base moles first; then decide what species control pH after the reaction.
common_point_loss: Starting with Henderson-Hasselbalch before checking whether both buffer components remain.

title: Acid-Base Titrations
what_it_is: A titration curve shows pH changes as titrant volume is added, with equivalence and half-equivalence points carrying key information.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using equivalence-point moles, identifying half-equivalence pH=pKa for weak titrations, and using major species to predict equivalence pH.
answer_move: Read the equivalence volume first; half of that volume gives pKa only for a weak acid/base titration.
common_point_loss: Using the total graph volume or equivalence-point pH as pKa.

title: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases
what_it_is: Molecular structure affects acid/base strength through conjugate-base stability and conjugate-acid weakness.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by relating stronger acid to more stable conjugate base and using structural features to justify that stability.
answer_move: Compare the conjugate bases, not just the acids, when explaining relative acid strength.
common_point_loss: Saying more H atoms automatically means a stronger acid.

title: pH and pKa
what_it_is: Comparing pH with pKa predicts whether the acid or base form of a conjugate pair dominates.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using pH<pKa for acid form dominance and pH>pKa for base form dominance, and by choosing indicators near equivalence pH.
answer_move: Compare pH to pKa before deciding protonated or deprotonated form.
common_point_loss: Reversing the dominance rule when pH is above pKa.

title: Properties of Buffers
what_it_is: Buffers resist pH change because they contain appreciable conjugate acid and conjugate base that consume added base or acid.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying both buffer components and explaining how each responds to added acid or base.
answer_move: Name the conjugate acid and conjugate base, then state which one reacts with the added stress.
common_point_loss: Calling any weak acid solution a buffer even when its conjugate base is absent.

title: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
what_it_is: Henderson-Hasselbalch relates buffer pH to pKa and the conjugate base to acid ratio.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using pH=pKa+log([A-]/[HA]) and solving the ratio with base over acid.
answer_move: Isolate [A-]/[HA] as 10^(pH-pKa), not with natural logs or a negative exponent.
common_point_loss: Solving the ratio as 10^-(pH-pKa) or using ln instead of log base 10.

title: Buffer Capacity
what_it_is: Buffer capacity is the amount of acid or base a buffer can absorb before pH changes substantially.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating pH, which depends on ratio, from capacity, which depends on amounts.
answer_move: Hold the ratio and total concentration ideas separately: ratio sets pH; amount sets capacity.
common_point_loss: Saying dilution that preserves ratio leaves buffer capacity unchanged.

title: pH and Solubility
what_it_is: Salt solubility can depend on pH when an ion reacts as a weak acid, weak base, or hydroxide.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the ion affected by acid or base and predicting whether dissolution is favored.
answer_move: Ask whether H+ or OH- removes one dissolved ion; if so, more solid can dissolve.
common_point_loss: Trying to compute pH-dependent solubility when qualitative reasoning is requested.

title: Introduction to Entropy
what_it_is: Entropy increases when matter or energy becomes more dispersed among more possible arrangements.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by naming gas moles, phase dispersal, volume, temperature, or energy distribution changes and linking them to microstates.
answer_move: Explain what particles or energy are becoming more dispersed.
common_point_loss: Saying only more disorder without a particle-level justification.

title: Absolute Entropy and Entropy Change
what_it_is: Standard entropy changes are calculated as products minus reactants using tabulated absolute entropy values.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by multiplying each standard entropy by coefficients and subtracting reactant sum from product sum.
answer_move: Set up products minus reactants with coefficients before calculating.
common_point_loss: Forgetting coefficients or reversing the subtraction.

title: Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability
what_it_is: Delta G combines enthalpy and entropy to decide whether a process is thermodynamically favored.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by calculating or reasoning from Delta H, Delta S, and T and using thermodynamically favored when Delta G is negative.
answer_move: Check which term favors negative Delta G before claiming the process is favored.
common_point_loss: Claiming both terms favor the process when only one sign supports negative Delta G.

title: Thermodynamic and Kinetic Control
what_it_is: A thermodynamically favored process may be too slow to observe if it has a large kinetic barrier.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing Delta G favorability from activation-energy-controlled rate.
answer_move: State whether the issue is thermodynamic direction or kinetic rate barrier.
common_point_loss: Saying a favored reaction that is slow must be at equilibrium.

title: Free Energy and Equilibrium
what_it_is: Standard free energy and K are linked: negative Delta G standard means products favored and K greater than 1.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using Delta G standard = -RT ln K and interpreting sign and magnitude correctly.
answer_move: Translate Delta G sign into K relative to 1 before doing detailed interpretation.
common_point_loss: Saying Delta G near zero means no reaction rather than K near 1.

title: Free Energy of Dissolution
what_it_is: Dissolution favorability depends on competing enthalpy and entropy effects from separating solute, reorganizing solvent, and forming solute-solvent interactions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the three contributions and explaining why the total Delta G may be favorable or unfavorable.
answer_move: Break dissolution into solute separation, solvent reorganization, and solute-solvent attraction before judging favorability.
common_point_loss: Assuming every dissolving process is entropy-favored and therefore always favored.

title: Coupled Reactions
what_it_is: An unfavorable process can be driven by coupling it to a favorable process or external energy source.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by showing the combined process has negative net Delta G or by identifying the external energy input.
answer_move: Add the Delta G values for coupled steps and decide whether the net process is favored.
common_point_loss: Calling the unfavorable step favored just because it occurs when coupled.

title: Galvanic and Electrolytic Cells
what_it_is: Electrochemical cells separate oxidation and reduction into half-cells connected by electron and ion flow paths.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying anode/cathode by process, explaining salt bridge and electron flow roles, and not relying on electrode positive/negative labels.
answer_move: Assign anode and cathode from oxidation and reduction, not from charge labels.
common_point_loss: Assuming cathode always means the same metal role from an earlier part of a question.

title: Cell Potential and Free Energy
what_it_is: Cell potential measures redox driving force, with positive E for thermodynamically favored cell reactions and Delta G = -nFE.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing cathode/anode from reduction potentials, calculating E cell, and connecting sign to Delta G and favorability.
answer_move: Choose the reduction with greater reduction potential for the cathode in a galvanic cell; then calculate E cell.
common_point_loss: Forgetting that a metal can switch electrode roles when paired with a different half-reaction.

title: Cell Potential under Nonstandard Conditions
what_it_is: Nonstandard cell potential depends on reaction composition and decreases toward zero as the cell approaches equilibrium.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using Q qualitatively, explaining concentration effects on driving force, and recognizing E=0 at equilibrium.
answer_move: Relate concentration changes to Q, then explain whether the cell is farther from or closer to equilibrium.
common_point_loss: Using Le Chatelier equilibrium-shift language as if the electrochemical cell were already at equilibrium.

title: Electrolysis and Faraday's Law
what_it_is: Faraday law connects current, time, electrons transferred, ion charge, and mass plated or removed at an electrode.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using I=q/t, converting charge to moles of electrons, using ion charge for mole ratios, and converting moles to mass.
answer_move: Convert current and time to charge, charge to electrons, electrons to substance, then substance to mass.
common_point_loss: Ignoring ion charge when converting electrons to moles of metal plated.

title: Scalars and Vectors in One Dimension
what_it_is: A scalar is a quantity with only a size (like speed or distance), while a vector has both size and direction (like velocity or displacement). In one dimension, direction collapses down to a plus or minus sign along a chosen axis.
how_points_are_earned: Credit comes from consistently assigning and using a sign convention (e.g., positive = rightward or upward) for every vector quantity in a problem, and from correctly identifying which given quantities are scalars (speed, distance, time) versus vectors (velocity, displacement, acceleration).
answer_move: Before solving, state your positive direction in words or with an arrow, then attach the correct sign to every velocity, displacement, and acceleration value you write down -- a bare number without an implied or stated sign is not a complete vector value in 1-D.
common_point_loss: Treating speed and velocity as interchangeable, or dropping the negative sign on a value once it's plugged into an equation.

title: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration
what_it_is: Displacement (delta-x = x - x0) is the change in position; average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time; average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by elapsed time. Instantaneous velocity and acceleration are what those averages approach as you shrink the time interval to something very small.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly computing displacement, change in velocity, average velocity, or average acceleration from given position/velocity/time data, and from correctly distinguishing an instantaneous value (read at one moment) from an average value (computed over an interval).
answer_move: When a problem gives you two positions or two velocities at two different times, explicitly compute the change (final minus initial) before dividing by the elapsed time -- don't skip straight to a memorized formula without showing the subtraction that defines it.
common_point_loss: Reporting a velocity or acceleration found from a slope calculation as if it were instantaneous when the problem actually asked for (or gave data for) an average over an interval.

title: Representing Motion
what_it_is: This topic covers the three constant-acceleration kinematic equations and how motion appears on position-time, velocity-time, and acceleration-time graphs -- slopes give instantaneous rates, and areas give net changes.
how_points_are_earned: Points require selecting the kinematic equation that matches the known and unknown quantities, substituting correctly, and -- for graph items -- correctly matching slope-of-position-graph to velocity, slope-of-velocity-graph to acceleration, area-under-velocity-graph to displacement, and area-under-acceleration-graph to change in velocity; nonuniform-acceleration graphs are scored on qualitative shape/reasoning, not on plugging into the three equations.
answer_move: Before using a constant-acceleration equation, confirm acceleration is actually constant over the interval in question -- if the acceleration is changing, switch to reading slopes and areas off the graph instead, since the constant-acceleration equations don't apply there.
common_point_loss: Plugging numbers into a constant-acceleration equation for a motion segment where the acceleration is actually changing, instead of switching to graphical/qualitative reasoning.

title: Reference Frames and Relative Motion
what_it_is: A reference frame is the viewpoint (moving or stationary) from which motion is measured. Acceleration comes out the same in every inertial frame, but velocity does not -- an object's velocity in one frame differs from its velocity in another by the relative velocity between the frames.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly adding or subtracting one-dimensional velocities to convert between reference frames, and from correctly stating that the acceleration of an object is the same as measured in any inertial frame.
answer_move: When a problem gives motion relative to a moving frame (like a person walking on a moving walkway) restricted to one dimension, add the object's velocity in that frame to the frame's own velocity (with correct signs) to get velocity in the ground frame -- do not attempt this as a two-dimensional vector-addition problem, since 2-D relative-velocity situations are outside this course.
common_point_loss: Trying to combine relative velocities using two-dimensional vector addition (like a boat crossing a river) when this course only holds students responsible for one-dimensional relative motion.

title: Vectors and Motion in Two Dimensions
what_it_is: Two-dimensional motion, most often projectile motion, is analyzed by resolving vectors into perpendicular components using right-triangle trigonometry, then treating each axis as its own independent one-dimensional motion problem.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly resolving an initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components, recognizing horizontal acceleration is zero while vertical acceleration is constant, and solving each axis with the appropriate 1-D kinematic equation before recombining results if needed.
answer_move: For projectile motion, split the initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components immediately, then solve the vertical axis (constant acceleration) and horizontal axis (constant velocity) as two separate 1-D kinematics problems linked only by a shared time variable.
common_point_loss: Using the initial launch speed directly in a kinematics equation instead of first resolving it into horizontal and vertical components.

title: Systems and Center of Mass
what_it_is: A system is the selected object or group of objects. Center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of that system.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the system, using mass-weighted position sums, and staying within the five-particle or high-symmetry center-of-mass boundary.
answer_move: Draw the system boundary first, then write the center-of-mass sum with each mass and position that belongs inside the system.
common_point_loss: Using the geometric middle as center of mass without checking where the mass is located.

title: Forces and Free-Body Diagrams
what_it_is: A free-body diagram shows the real forces exerted on one object, drawn as arrows from the object dot. Components are not drawn as extra force arrows.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the object, drawing each external force once, labeling forces clearly, and resolving components only after the FBD is complete.
answer_move: Start with the object dot and draw only real forces on that object; make component equations separately.
common_point_loss: Drawing both a force and its components on the FBD, which double-counts the interaction.

title: Newton's Third Law
what_it_is: Newton's third law pairs are equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces exerted on different objects in the same interaction.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by naming force pairs as A on B and B on A, assigning each force to the object it acts on, and identifying internal versus external forces for a system.
answer_move: Write the two object names in every interaction pair before deciding which free-body diagram receives each force.
common_point_loss: Putting both action-reaction forces on the same free-body diagram.

title: Newton's First Law
what_it_is: Newton's first law says velocity is constant when net force is zero in an inertial frame. Equilibrium can apply in one direction while another direction accelerates.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by linking zero acceleration to zero net force along the relevant axis and by not erasing balanced forces that still act on the object.
answer_move: Check acceleration component by component; if acceleration is zero along an axis, set the net force along that axis to zero.
common_point_loss: Saying there are no forces because the object moves with constant velocity.

title: Newton's Second Law
what_it_is: Newton's second law connects net force to acceleration: a_sys = F_net/m_sys. The force sum must match the object or system mass in the equation.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing the FBD, writing component net-force equations for the selected object or system, and using constraints only on separate lines.
answer_move: After the FBD, write sum F = ma for the same object or system named in the diagram.
common_point_loss: Mixing forces from different objects into one equation without using the total system mass.

title: Gravitational Force
what_it_is: Gravitational force is attractive, acts along the line between centers of mass, and can be modeled as F_g = Gm1m2/r^2 or as weight mg near Earth.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing force, field, weight, and apparent weight, using the correct masses and separation, and remembering that larger planet mass increases g at the same radius.
answer_move: Identify what the question asks for: gravitational force, gravitational field, weight, or apparent weight; then choose the matching equation.
common_point_loss: Confusing mass with weight or treating apparent weight as always equal to mg.

title: Kinetic and Static Friction
what_it_is: Kinetic friction is mu_k F_N while surfaces slide. Static friction adjusts up to a maximum, so F_s is less than or equal to mu_s F_N.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by deciding kinetic versus static contact, setting kinetic friction as an equality, solving for needed static friction first, and checking it against its maximum.
answer_move: Ask whether the surfaces slide; if they do not, solve for the static friction needed before comparing to mu_s F_N.
common_point_loss: Setting static friction equal to mu_s F_N whenever the object is not moving.

title: Spring Forces
what_it_is: An ideal spring exerts a restoring force F_s = -k Delta x, directed toward the spring-system equilibrium position.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by measuring displacement from equilibrium, using the spring constant, and assigning the restoring direction before writing force equations.
answer_move: Mark equilibrium first, then draw the spring force back toward equilibrium and use magnitude k Delta x in the force equation.
common_point_loss: Using total spring length instead of displacement from equilibrium.

title: Circular Motion
what_it_is: Circular motion has centripetal acceleration v^2/r toward the center. Real forces or force components provide the inward net force.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing real forces on the FBD, choosing inward as radial, writing sum F_radial = mv^2/r, and not drawing centripetal force as an extra force.
answer_move: Draw the FBD first, then choose inward as positive and identify which real force or component supplies the radial net force.
common_point_loss: Adding a separate centripetal-force arrow to the FBD instead of using real forces.

title: Translational Kinetic Energy
what_it_is: Translational Kinetic Energy is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: compute kinetic energy from mass and speed and recognize that it depends on reference frame.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you compute kinetic energy from mass and speed and recognize that it depends on reference frame, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then compute kinetic energy from mass and speed and recognize that it depends on reference frame before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Using velocity direction to make kinetic energy negative

title: Work
what_it_is: Work is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: find signed work from the force component parallel to displacement or from area under an F-parallel versus displacement graph.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you find signed work from the force component parallel to displacement or from area under an F-parallel versus displacement graph, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then find signed work from the force component parallel to displacement or from area under an F-parallel versus displacement graph before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Using total force magnitude when only the parallel component does work

what_it_is: Potential Energy is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: choose a system and calculate gravitational or spring potential-energy changes from configuration.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you choose a system and calculate gravitational or spring potential-energy changes from configuration, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then choose a system and calculate gravitational or spring potential-energy changes from configuration before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.

how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you write an initial-energy equals final-energy plus transfer or dissipation equation for the chosen system, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.

how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you relate average power to energy transfer per time and instantaneous power to the parallel force component times speed, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
