title: Linear Momentum
what_it_is: Linear momentum is p = mv: mass times velocity. Because velocity is a vector, momentum is also a vector in the same direction as the object velocity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by computing momentum with velocity signs or directions, summing system momentum as a vector quantity, and recognizing that momentum is linear momentum unless the prompt says otherwise.
answer_move: Set a positive direction before writing p = mv; then attach that sign or direction to each object momentum before adding system totals.
common_point_loss: Adding momentum magnitudes and losing the direction of one object motion.

title: Change in Momentum and Impulse
what_it_is: Impulse is the change in momentum: J = delta p = F_avg delta t. On a net-force-versus-time graph, impulse is the signed area under the curve.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by calculating delta p as final momentum minus initial momentum, finding impulse from average force times time or graph area, and matching impulse direction to net force direction.
answer_move: Write delta p = p_f - p_i before using any impulse equation; if a force-time graph is given, find signed area instead of multiplying one force reading by total time.
common_point_loss: Using p = Ft as if momentum equals force times time, instead of impulse or change in momentum equaling force-time area.

title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
what_it_is: Total momentum of a chosen system stays constant when the net external impulse on that system is zero. Internal forces can exchange momentum between objects but cannot change the system total.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the system, checking external impulse, summing initial and final momentum with signs, and using conservation only for the selected system.
answer_move: Draw a boundary around the system first; if the net external impulse is zero, set total initial momentum equal to total final momentum and keep directions signed.
common_point_loss: Saying momentum is conserved for one object during a collision instead of for the whole interacting system.

title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
what_it_is: Collisions are classified by kinetic energy behavior. Elastic collisions conserve system kinetic energy; inelastic collisions do not; perfectly inelastic collisions are the special case where objects stick together and share one final velocity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by conserving momentum for the system, checking whether total kinetic energy is the same before and after, and identifying perfectly inelastic collisions from shared final motion.
answer_move: Use momentum conservation to find or compare final velocities, then separately compare total kinetic energy to classify the collision; do not use kinetic-energy conservation unless the collision is elastic.
common_point_loss: Assuming momentum is not conserved in inelastic collisions because kinetic energy decreases.

title: Rotational Kinematics
what_it_is: Rotational kinematics describes angular position, angular velocity, and angular acceleration for rotation about an axis, using clockwise or counterclockwise signs.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the rotation axis, choosing CW or CCW as positive, using radians, and applying angular kinematics equations with signs consistently.
answer_move: Choose the axis and positive rotational direction first; then use theta, omega, and alpha the same way you use x, v, and a in linear kinematics.
common_point_loss: Mixing clockwise and counterclockwise signs after writing the angular kinematics equation.

title: Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion
what_it_is: Points on a rotating rigid system connect angular and linear motion through s = r theta, v = r omega, and a_T = r alpha.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the radius of the specific point, keeping angular quantities common to the rigid body, and using tangential acceleration rather than total acceleration.
answer_move: Identify the point and its distance from the axis before using v = r omega or a_T = r alpha.
common_point_loss: Using the same linear speed for every point on a rotating rigid object because they share the same angular speed.

title: Torque
what_it_is: Torque measures how effectively a force causes rotation about an axis. Its magnitude is tau = rF_perp = rF sin(theta), or force times lever arm.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the axis, measuring r from axis to force point, using only the perpendicular force component or lever arm, and applying CW/CCW signs when needed.
answer_move: Draw the line of action of the force, find the perpendicular lever arm from the axis, then compute tau magnitude and assign CW or CCW tendency.
common_point_loss: Multiplying force by the full distance to the axis when the force is not perpendicular.

title: Rotational Inertia
what_it_is: Rotational inertia measures resistance to angular acceleration. For point masses, I = mr^2 and total rotational inertia is the sum of each m r^2 term.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by measuring each mass distance from the rotation axis, summing m r^2 for allowed point-mass systems, and reasoning qualitatively about mass distribution.
answer_move: Locate the axis first, then compute each point mass contribution with its own radius before adding them.
common_point_loss: Using total mass times one average radius squared without checking each object distance from the axis.

title: Rotational Equilibrium and Newton's First Law in Rotational Form
what_it_is: Rotational equilibrium means net torque is zero, so angular velocity is constant. A system can be in rotational equilibrium without being in translational equilibrium, or vice versa.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing an axis, summing CW and CCW torques, setting net torque to zero for rotational equilibrium, and separately checking translational equilibrium if asked.
answer_move: Write one torque-balance equation about a chosen axis; use signs for CW and CCW tendencies and do not assume force balance alone is enough.
common_point_loss: Saying an object is in rotational equilibrium just because the net force is zero.

title: Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form
what_it_is: Newton's second law in rotational form is alpha = tau_net/I_sys. Net torque causes angular acceleration, with rotational inertia resisting the change.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by finding net torque about the axis, using the system rotational inertia about that axis, and solving for angular acceleration with correct signs.
answer_move: After drawing forces, write tau_net about the rotation axis, then divide by I_sys to get alpha.
common_point_loss: Using net force divided by mass for a rotating object when the question asks for angular acceleration.

title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
what_it_is: Rotational kinetic energy is the energy a system has because it rotates: K = 1/2 I omega^2. Total kinetic energy can include both translational and rotational parts.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying every kinetic-energy term, using I about the correct axis, and adding 1/2 mv^2 and 1/2 I omega^2 only when both motions occur.
answer_move: Before writing energy conservation, list translational KE and rotational KE separately, then decide which terms belong before and after.
common_point_loss: Counting only 1/2 mv^2 for a rolling or spinning rigid object that also has rotational kinetic energy.

title: Torque and Work
what_it_is: A torque does work when it acts through an angular displacement. For constant torque, W = tau Delta theta; for changing torque, work is area under a torque-vs-angle graph.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using angular displacement in radians, matching torque sign to the rotation, or finding signed area under a torque-position graph.
answer_move: Translate the situation into rotational work: identify tau, Delta theta, and whether graph area or tau Delta theta gives the energy transfer.
common_point_loss: Multiplying torque by linear distance instead of angular displacement, or treating graph height alone as work.

title: Angular Momentum and Angular Impulse
what_it_is: Angular momentum measures rotational motion about a chosen axis or point. In AP Physics 1, use magnitudes such as L = I omega or L = rmv sin(theta).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by naming the axis or point, using the correct magnitude expression, and connecting angular impulse to Delta L or area under a torque-vs-time graph.
answer_move: State the reference axis or point first; then use L = I omega for rotating rigid systems or L = rmv sin(theta) for a moving object about a point.
common_point_loss: Writing angular momentum without specifying the reference axis or point, then treating it as a universal object property.

title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
what_it_is: Angular momentum is conserved for a chosen system when the net external torque about the chosen axis is zero. Internal changes can redistribute angular momentum.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the system, checking external torque about the axis, and setting initial total angular momentum equal to final total angular momentum only when justified.
answer_move: Ask whether the external torque about the chosen axis is zero; if it is, conserve total angular momentum for the system, not necessarily angular speed.
common_point_loss: Conserving angular speed instead of angular momentum when rotational inertia changes.

title: Rolling
what_it_is: Rolling motion combines translation of the center of mass with rotation about the center. Without slipping, v_cm = r omega and K_total = K_trans + K_rot.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by separating translational and rotational motion, applying v_cm = r omega only for rolling without slipping, and including both kinetic-energy terms when needed.
answer_move: Label whether the object rolls without slipping; then use v_cm = r omega and K = 1/2 mv_cm^2 + 1/2 I omega^2 only when that condition applies.
common_point_loss: Using v_cm = r omega for a slipping object, where center-of-mass motion and rotation are not directly linked.

title: Motion of Orbiting Satellites
what_it_is: Orbiting-satellite motion uses gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and angular momentum for a satellite around a much more massive central object.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the satellite-central-object system, using U_g = -Gm1m2/r with zero at infinity, and applying energy or angular-momentum conservation to the orbit type.
answer_move: Identify circular versus elliptical motion first, then decide which quantities are constant and which energy terms can change with orbital radius.
common_point_loss: Treating gravitational potential energy as zero at the planet surface or assuming speed is constant in every orbit.

title: Defining Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
what_it_is: Simple harmonic motion is periodic motion caused by a restoring force that points toward equilibrium and has magnitude proportional to displacement from equilibrium.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying equilibrium, displacement from equilibrium, restoring-force direction, and proportionality between restoring-force magnitude and displacement.
answer_move: Start by marking equilibrium, then state that the restoring force points opposite displacement and grows with distance from equilibrium.
common_point_loss: Calling any back-and-forth periodic motion SHM without showing a proportional restoring force.

title: Frequency and Period of SHM
what_it_is: Period is the time for one complete cycle and frequency is cycles per second, with T = 1/f. For SHM, spring and small-angle pendulum periods come from system parameters.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using T = 1/f, selecting the correct period model, and explaining variable changes from the formula instead of from intuition about speed or amplitude.
answer_move: Identify the oscillator type first; use T_s = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) for a spring-object system and T_p = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) for a small-angle pendulum.
common_point_loss: Putting amplitude into the period formula or treating frequency and period as directly proportional.

title: Representing and Analyzing SHM
what_it_is: SHM can be represented with sinusoidal position-time graphs such as x = A cos(2 pi f t) or x = A sin(2 pi f t), along with related velocity and acceleration behavior.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading amplitude, period, frequency, signs, extrema, and zero crossings from graphs and by connecting acceleration direction to displacement from equilibrium.
answer_move: Use the position graph as the anchor: amplitude is maximum displacement, one cycle gives period, and velocity is greatest as the oscillator passes equilibrium.
common_point_loss: Reading a large amplitude as a longer period even though changing amplitude does not change period for SHM.

title: Energy of Simple Harmonic Oscillators
what_it_is: In an ideal simple harmonic oscillator, total mechanical energy stays constant while kinetic energy and potential energy trade back and forth during the cycle.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by locating where K and U are maximum or minimum, using conservation of total energy, and relating larger amplitude to larger total oscillator energy.
answer_move: Mark turning points and equilibrium first; at turning points K = 0 and U is maximum, while at equilibrium spring PE is minimum and K is maximum.
common_point_loss: Saying energy is lost at the turning point because the oscillator momentarily stops.

title: Internal Structure and Density
what_it_is: Density is mass per volume, rho = m/V, and a fluid is a substance with no fixed shape. An ideal fluid is modeled as incompressible and nonviscous.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by distinguishing solids, liquids, and gases by particle interactions, computing density from mass and volume, and naming both ideal-fluid assumptions when used.
answer_move: State rho = m/V with units, then decide whether the situation allows the ideal-fluid model: incompressible and no viscosity.
common_point_loss: Treating ideal fluid as only incompressible and forgetting the no-viscosity assumption.

title: Pressure
what_it_is: Pressure is perpendicular force per area, P = F_perp/A, and it is a scalar. In a static fluid, pressure can increase with depth as P = P0 + rho gh.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using perpendicular force, area, density, depth, and reference pressure correctly and by distinguishing absolute pressure from gauge pressure.
answer_move: Draw the surface area receiving the force, use the perpendicular component, and choose P = P0 + rho gh or P_gauge = rho gh based on what the prompt asks.
common_point_loss: Using total force direction or object volume instead of perpendicular force over contact area.

title: Fluids and Newton's Laws
what_it_is: Newton's laws still apply to fluids and objects in fluids. Buoyant force is the upward net force from fluid interactions and equals the weight of displaced fluid.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing forces on the object or fluid element, applying Newton's second law to the selected object/system, and calculating buoyant force as rho V g for displaced fluid.
answer_move: Start with a force diagram: weight downward, buoyant force upward, and any applied or contact forces; then write net force from those forces.
common_point_loss: Using the object mass in the buoyant-force expression instead of the displaced fluid density and displaced volume.

title: Fluids and Conservation Laws
what_it_is: Conservation laws describe ideal-fluid flow: continuity conserves mass flow rate, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and Bernoulli relates pressure, height, and speed along a flow.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking ideal-fluid and filled-pipe assumptions, applying continuity between cross sections, and using Bernoulli or Torricelli with consistent heights and pressures.
answer_move: Use continuity first when areas and speeds are linked; then apply Bernoulli between two points with clearly chosen y values, pressures, and speeds.
common_point_loss: Assuming higher speed always means higher pressure without applying Bernoulli with height and reference points.

title: Kinetic Theory: Temperature and Pressure
what_it_is: Gas pressure comes from atoms colliding with a surface -- it's the perpendicular force per area those collisions produce, and it exists at every point inside the gas, not just at the container wall. Temperature is a measure of the atoms' average kinetic energy, and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows how that energy is spread across all the atoms at a given temperature.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly relating pressure to atomic collisions, computing or reasoning with the kinetic-energy-temperature relation, and reading qualitative features of a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve (peak location, spread, high-speed tail) to compare two temperatures or two gas samples.
answer_move: When asked to compare two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves or describe how one changes with temperature, describe the shift and spread in words (peak moves to higher speed, curve flattens and widens) -- do not attempt to state or use a mathematical formula for the distribution itself, since this course only requires qualitative reading of its shape.
common_point_loss: Describing pressure as something that only exists 'at the walls' instead of throughout the gas, or treating a higher Maxwell-Boltzmann peak speed as the only thing that changes with temperature while ignoring the spread.

title: The Ideal Gas Law
what_it_is: The ideal gas law connects a gas's pressure, volume, temperature, and quantity of particles under the idealizations that atoms have negligible volume, move randomly, and collide elastically.
how_points_are_earned: Points require correctly solving the ideal gas law for an unknown variable with consistent units (temperature in kelvin), reading values off pressure-volume, pressure-temperature, or volume-temperature graphs, and extrapolating a linear pressure-vs-temperature graph back to zero pressure to estimate absolute zero.
answer_move: When a pressure-vs-temperature graph is given and the question asks for the temperature at which pressure would reach zero, extend the straight-line trend down to the temperature axis rather than assuming the answer must be zero Celsius or reading only the plotted data range.
common_point_loss: Plugging a Celsius temperature directly into the ideal gas law instead of converting to kelvin first.

title: Thermal Energy Transfer and Equilibrium
what_it_is: Two objects in thermal contact can exchange energy by conduction, convection, or radiation; energy spontaneously flows from the higher-temperature system to the lower-temperature one until both reach the same temperature, a state called thermal equilibrium where net energy transfer stops.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly identifying the direction of spontaneous energy transfer (hot to cold, never the reverse), naming or distinguishing the transfer mechanism appropriate to a scenario, and stating that thermal equilibrium means zero net energy transfer, not zero atomic motion.
answer_move: When asked to explain why two objects at different temperatures reach a common final temperature, frame it as the statistically most probable outcome of many random atomic collisions redistributing energy -- not as 'heat rising' or objects 'wanting' to equalize.
common_point_loss: Describing thermal equilibrium as a state where atoms stop moving, rather than a state where net energy transfer between the two systems has stopped.

title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
what_it_is: The first law is energy conservation applied to a gas's internal energy: internal energy changes because thermal energy is transferred in/out or work is done on/by the gas as its volume changes. PV diagrams let you visualize a process, and the area under the curve gives the magnitude of work done.
how_points_are_earned: Points require correctly applying the sign conventions in the first law, computing work from a constant/average pressure and volume change (or the area under a P-V curve) for a given process, identifying which quantity is zero or constant for isovolumetric/isothermal/isobaric/adiabatic processes, and computing internal energy change for a monatomic ideal gas.
answer_move: When a process is labeled adiabatic, immediately set the heat transfer to zero and get the internal energy change entirely from work -- don't try to estimate any thermal energy transfer for that step, since by definition none occurs.
common_point_loss: Forgetting the negative sign in the work-from-pressure-and-volume-change formula, so an expanding gas (doing positive work on its surroundings) is incorrectly recorded as gaining energy from work instead of losing it.

title: Specific Heat and Thermal Conductivity
what_it_is: Specific heat tells you how much thermal energy changes a material's temperature; thermal conductivity tells you how fast thermal energy passes through a material of a given thickness and area. Both are fixed properties of the material.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly using the specific-heat equation to find heat, mass, specific heat, or temperature change (including setting heat lost equal to heat gained in two-object mixing problems), using the conduction-rate equation to find conduction rate, and treating specific heat as constant across the whole temperature change in a problem.
answer_move: In any calorimetry problem, set the heat lost by the warmer object equal to the heat gained by the cooler object and solve -- do not average the two starting temperatures as a shortcut, since masses and specific heats can differ.
common_point_loss: Assuming specific heat changes as an object's temperature changes, instead of treating it as constant throughout the process as this course requires.

title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
what_it_is: Entropy is a measure of how spread out or unavailable-to-do-work energy has become; it depends only on a system's current configuration, not its history. The second law says an isolated system's total entropy never decreases and stays constant only if every process in it is reversible.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from qualitatively explaining why total entropy of an isolated system increases or stays the same for a given process, correctly identifying that a non-isolated (closed) system's entropy can decrease because energy crosses its boundary, and connecting maximum entropy to thermodynamic equilibrium -- all in words, with no quantitative entropy calculation expected.
answer_move: When asked to justify an entropy claim, explain it in terms of energy dispersal and probability (energy spreading among more possible configurations is far more likely than it spontaneously concentrating) -- never attempt a numeric entropy calculation, since this course tests entropy only qualitatively.
common_point_loss: Claiming a single closed (non-isolated) part of a larger system can never lose entropy, when only the total entropy of a fully isolated system is guaranteed not to decrease.

title: Electric Charge and Electric Force
what_it_is: Electric charge is a positive or negative property of matter, and charged objects exert forces on each other through Coulomb law.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying charge sign, using Coulomb law for magnitude, setting force direction along the line between charges, and vector-adding forces for four or fewer charges unless symmetry is given.
answer_move: Draw the line between charges first; then decide attraction or repulsion before calculating magnitude.
common_point_loss: Calculating the correct Coulomb magnitude but giving the force direction as if all charges repel.

title: Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging
what_it_is: Net charge is conserved for an isolated system, while friction, contact, induction, and grounding redistribute or transfer charge.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by conserving total charge, distinguishing transfer from polarization, identifying electron movement, and explaining grounding as connection to a large neutral reservoir.
answer_move: Choose the system first; then track where electrons move and whether net charge changes or only redistributes.
common_point_loss: Saying a neutral object becomes charged by creating positive charge rather than by separating or transferring charge.

title: Electric Fields
what_it_is: An electric field gives the force per unit positive test charge at each point and is found by vector superposition from source charges.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using E = F_E/q, drawing field direction away from positive and toward negative sources, vector-adding fields for four or fewer charges unless symmetry is given, and applying conductor equilibrium facts.
answer_move: At the point of interest, draw each source field vector as if a positive test charge were placed there; then add vectors.
common_point_loss: Using the sign of the test charge to reverse the electric field direction instead of reversing only the force on that charge.

title: Electric Potential Energy
what_it_is: Electric potential energy is energy stored in a configuration of charges, with point-charge pairs contributing U_E = k q1 q2/r.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by summing pairwise potential energies for four or fewer point charges, preserving charge signs, and connecting changes in U_E to work or kinetic energy.
answer_move: List every interacting pair once; then use signed charges in U_E before summing the total.
common_point_loss: Using absolute values in electric potential energy and losing the sign that tells whether the interaction is attractive or repulsive.

title: Electric Potential
what_it_is: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge, and potentials from point charges add as scalars.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using V = k sum(q_i/r_i), applying Delta V = Delta U_E/q, reading equipotential spacing and direction, and remembering there is no field component along an equipotential line.
answer_move: Treat potential as a signed scalar first; then use field direction and equipotential geometry after the potential comparison is clear.
common_point_loss: Vector-adding electric potential the way electric field vectors are added.

title: Capacitors
what_it_is: A capacitor separates equal and opposite charge, with capacitance C = Q/Delta V set by geometry and material rather than by the amount of stored charge.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using C = Q/Delta V, C = kappa epsilon_0 A/d for parallel plates, E = Q/(kappa epsilon_0 A), U_C = 1/2 Q Delta V, and dielectric effects within AP scope.
answer_move: Identify what is held fixed first: charge, voltage, geometry, or dielectric. Then decide how C, Q, Delta V, field, and energy respond.
common_point_loss: Saying capacitance increases because more charge was placed on the plates, instead of because geometry or dielectric changed.

title: Conservation of Electric Energy
what_it_is: A charge moving through a potential difference changes electric potential energy by Delta U_E = q Delta V, with energy transferred to or from kinetic energy.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using signed Delta U_E = q Delta V, applying energy conservation, and deciding whether the electric field speeds up or slows down the charge.
answer_move: Write the initial and final potentials, compute signed Delta U_E, then let energy conservation decide the kinetic-energy change.
common_point_loss: Assuming a positive potential difference always increases kinetic energy without checking the sign of the moving charge.

title: Electric Current
what_it_is: Electric Current is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: relate current to charge flow per time and describe conventional current direction without treating current as a vector.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you relate current to charge flow per time and describe conventional current direction without treating current as a vector, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then relate current to charge flow per time and describe conventional current direction without treating current as a vector before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Adding currents like vector components rather than as scalar flow rates through circuit branches

title: Simple Circuits
what_it_is: Simple Circuits is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: translate between physical circuits and schematics using conventional-current assumptions.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you translate between physical circuits and schematics using conventional-current assumptions, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then translate between physical circuits and schematics using conventional-current assumptions before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Calling an open switch a closed current path

title: Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law
what_it_is: Resistance, Resistivity, and Ohm's Law is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: use R equals rho ell over A, Ohm's law, and graph slopes to connect material, geometry, current, and potential difference.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you use R equals rho ell over A, Ohm's law, and graph slopes to connect material, geometry, current, and potential difference, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then use R equals rho ell over A, Ohm's law, and graph slopes to connect material, geometry, current, and potential difference before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Treating resistivity and resistance as the same quantity

title: Electric Power
what_it_is: Electric Power is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: compare energy-transfer rates with P equals I Delta V and derived resistor power forms.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you compare energy-transfer rates with P equals I Delta V and derived resistor power forms, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then compare energy-transfer rates with P equals I Delta V and derived resistor power forms before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Assuming the bulb with the greatest current is brightest without checking potential difference or power

title: Compound Direct Current (DC) Circuits
what_it_is: Compound Direct Current (DC) Circuits is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: reduce series and parallel resistor networks and reason about ideal meters, wires, and battery terminal voltage.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you reduce series and parallel resistor networks and reason about ideal meters, wires, and battery terminal voltage, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then reduce series and parallel resistor networks and reason about ideal meters, wires, and battery terminal voltage before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Treating parallel resistors as if the same current must pass through each branch

title: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule
what_it_is: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule is the Electric Circuits topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: write potential-difference changes around a closed loop that sum to zero.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you write potential-difference changes around a closed loop that sum to zero, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then write potential-difference changes around a closed loop that sum to zero before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Losing sign consistency when moving across batteries and resistors in a loop equation

title: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule

title: Magnetic Fields
what_it_is: A magnetic field is a vector field produced by magnetic dipoles or moving charge, not isolated magnetic monopoles. Field lines form loops and a compass aligns with the local field.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying north/south dipoles, drawing field direction, using field-line density qualitatively for strength, and describing alignment or attraction/repulsion correctly.
answer_move: Sketch the dipole first: outside a bar magnet the field points away from north and toward south, with closed loops through the magnet.
common_point_loss: Breaking a magnet into separate north and south monopoles instead of two smaller dipoles.

title: Magnetism and Moving Charges
what_it_is: A moving charged object can create a magnetic field and can feel magnetic force in an external field. The force magnitude is FB = qvB sin(theta).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the right-hand rule, including charge sign, applying the angle boundary for quantitative force, and separating electric and magnetic forces when both fields are present.
answer_move: Point fingers with velocity, curl toward B, then use the thumb for positive-charge force and reverse direction for a negative charge.
common_point_loss: Using qvB without checking whether velocity is parallel, perpendicular, or antiparallel to the magnetic field.

title: Magnetism and Current-Carrying Wires
what_it_is: A current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field around it and can experience force in an external magnetic field. For a long straight wire, B = mu0 I/(2 pi r).
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying the wire right-hand rule, recognizing tangent circular fields around straight wires, using B proportional to I/r, and adding fields by direction.
answer_move: For a straight wire, point your thumb with conventional current; curled fingers show the magnetic-field direction around the wire.
common_point_loss: Drawing the magnetic field from a straight current-carrying wire radially outward instead of tangent to circles around the wire.

title: Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's Law
what_it_is: Magnetic flux measures the perpendicular magnetic-field component through an area, PhiB = BA cos(theta). A changing flux induces emf according to Faraday's law.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the area vector, deciding whether flux is increasing or decreasing, applying Faraday's law, and using Lenz's law for induced current direction.
answer_move: Write the original flux direction, state whether its magnitude is increasing or decreasing, then choose the induced field that opposes that change.
common_point_loss: Choosing induced current direction from the external field direction alone instead of from the change in magnetic flux.

title: Reflection
what_it_is: Reflection redirects a light ray at a surface. The law of reflection says angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, with both angles measured from the surface normal.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing the normal, measuring both angles from that normal, distinguishing specular from diffuse reflection, and tracing ray paths consistently.
answer_move: Draw the normal first; then make theta_i and theta_r equal on opposite sides of the normal, not the surface.
common_point_loss: Measuring reflection angles from the mirror surface instead of from the normal.

title: Images Formed by Mirrors
what_it_is: Mirrors form images by reflected rays. Real images form where rays actually meet; virtual images form where reflected rays appear to diverge from.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing principal rays, applying 1/si + 1/so = 1/f when needed, and classifying image type, orientation, size, and location.
answer_move: Use a ray diagram to predict image type first, then use the mirror equation and magnification to calculate distances or size ratios.
common_point_loss: Calling a virtual image real because your eye can see it behind the mirror.

title: Refraction
what_it_is: Refraction is a ray direction change when light crosses into a medium where its speed changes. Index of refraction is n = c/v, and Snell's law relates the angles.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by measuring angles from the normal, applying n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), and identifying when total internal reflection is possible.
answer_move: Compare indices first: into higher n bends toward the normal; into lower n bends away, and total internal reflection can occur only from higher n to lower n.
common_point_loss: Saying a ray always bends toward the normal whenever it enters a new medium.

title: Images Formed by Lenses
what_it_is: Thin lenses form images by refracting rays. Convex lenses converge parallel rays; concave lenses diverge rays as if from a focal point.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the correct lens type, tracing principal rays, applying 1/si + 1/so = 1/f, and classifying real/virtual, upright/inverted, and size.
answer_move: Trace principal rays before calculating: parallel-through-focus, through center, and through or toward the focal point depending on lens type.
common_point_loss: Using mirror reflection rays for a lens problem instead of tracing refracted rays through the lens.

title: Properties of Wave Pulses and Waves
what_it_is: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Mechanical waves require a medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying transverse versus longitudinal motion, medium requirements, amplitude meaning, and how wave speed depends on medium properties.
answer_move: Name the wave type and medium first; then connect amplitude to energy and speed to the medium rather than to how hard the source shakes.
common_point_loss: Saying the medium travels with the wave instead of saying energy travels through the medium.

title: Periodic Waves
what_it_is: Periodic waves repeat with period T, frequency f, wavelength lambda, and speed v. The core relation is lambda = v/f.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by reading amplitude, period, frequency, and wavelength from graphs, using T = 1/f and lambda = v/f, and not tying amplitude to frequency.
answer_move: Decide whether the graph is displacement-vs-time or displacement-vs-position before reading period or wavelength.
common_point_loss: Reading wavelength from a time graph or period from a position graph.

title: Boundary Behavior of Waves and Polarization
what_it_is: At a boundary, waves may reflect, transmit, invert, refract, or become polarized. Frequency stays the same when a wave crosses into a new medium.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by comparing wave speeds across media, deciding whether reflected pulses invert, conserving frequency across boundaries, and applying polarization only to transverse waves.
answer_move: At a boundary, keep frequency fixed first; then decide how speed and wavelength change in the transmitted medium.
common_point_loss: Changing frequency when a wave enters a new medium.

title: Electromagnetic Waves
what_it_is: Electromagnetic waves are transverse oscillating electric and magnetic fields that can travel through vacuum at c and are ordered by wavelength across the EM spectrum.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by ordering EM categories and visible colors by wavelength or frequency, using c = lambda f in vacuum, and remembering EM waves do not need a medium.
answer_move: Use wavelength and frequency as inverse rankings: longer wavelength means lower frequency for EM waves in vacuum.
common_point_loss: Putting violet at the long-wavelength end of visible light or treating EM waves as requiring a medium.

title: The Doppler Effect
what_it_is: The Doppler effect is a qualitative frequency shift caused by source-observer relative motion: approaching raises observed frequency; receding lowers it.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by comparing observed and source frequency qualitatively and relating larger relative speed to a larger frequency difference.
answer_move: Ask whether source and observer move toward or away from each other; then state whether observed frequency is higher, lower, or unchanged.
common_point_loss: Trying to use a memorized Doppler formula or reversing approaching and receding shifts.

title: Wave Interference and Standing Waves
what_it_is: Interference superposes overlapping waves. Standing waves form from opposite-traveling waves in a confined region, producing nodes and antinodes.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by adding displacements, distinguishing constructive/destructive interference, identifying nodes/antinodes, and matching harmonics to boundary conditions.
answer_move: Mark the boundary conditions first; then locate nodes and antinodes before naming the harmonic.
common_point_loss: Treating every standing-wave pattern as if all integer harmonics are allowed, including node-antinode systems.

title: Diffraction
what_it_is: Diffraction is wave spreading around obstacles or through openings, strongest when the opening size is comparable to wavelength.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by relating spreading to opening size versus wavelength and using a sin(theta) or small-angle relations for minima when quantitative information is required.
answer_move: Compare opening width to wavelength first; then use the path-difference condition for dark bands in a single-opening pattern.
common_point_loss: Saying narrower openings make less diffraction because less light gets through.

title: Double-Slit Interference and Diffraction Gratings
what_it_is: Double-slit and grating patterns come from path-length differences between coherent light from multiple openings. Bright maxima occur where waves arrive in phase.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using d sin(theta) or d y/L path-difference reasoning, connecting larger wavelength to larger spacing, and not confusing maximum order with adjacent-fringe spacing.
answer_move: Write the path-length difference first; then connect constructive interference to integer multiples of wavelength.
common_point_loss: Using slit spacing as if it were the path-length difference at the screen.

title: Thin-Film Interference
what_it_is: Thin-film interference comes from two reflected rays that may gain phase shifts at boundaries and travel different distances through a film.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by tracking both reflected rays, identifying 180-degree phase shifts at higher-index reflections, including film-thickness path difference, and staying within normal-incidence quantitative scope.
answer_move: List the two reflected rays, mark any phase flip at each boundary, then compare their total phase difference.
common_point_loss: Ignoring phase changes at reflection and using only the extra distance through the film.

title: Quantum Theory and Wave-Particle Duality
what_it_is: Light energy comes in photons with E = hf, and matter can show wave behavior through the de Broglie relation lambda = h/p.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using E = hf and lambda = c/f for photons, using lambda = h/p for matter waves, and recognizing that bound systems have allowed energies rather than any arbitrary energy.
answer_move: Decide whether the object is a photon or a massive particle first; then choose the matching energy, wavelength, and momentum relations.
common_point_loss: Using lambda = h/p for a photon while also ignoring E = hf, or treating quantization as just a measurement limitation.

title: The Bohr Model of Atomic Structure
what_it_is: The Bohr model treats allowed electron states in a single-electron atom as standing-wave circular orbits with discrete energies.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using nuclear notation, identifying isotopes, connecting allowed Bohr states to standing-wave conditions, and keeping the discussion to single-electron energy-level diagrams.
answer_move: State the allowed-state idea first, then connect transitions between allowed levels to photon absorption or emission.
common_point_loss: Describing modern orbitals or probability clouds when the question is asking for the Bohr-model energy-level picture.

title: Emission and Absorption Spectra
what_it_is: Atoms emit or absorb photons only when the photon energy exactly matches the difference between two allowed energy levels.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by matching photon energy to Delta E, deciding whether a transition emits or absorbs light, and connecting larger energy gaps to higher-frequency photons.
answer_move: Write Delta E between the two levels, then set it equal to hf before deciding frequency, wavelength, or direction of transition.
common_point_loss: Saying an electron can absorb any photon with enough energy for every bound-to-bound transition.

title: Blackbody Radiation
what_it_is: A blackbody is an ideal absorber and emitter whose continuous spectrum depends on temperature and whose energy exchange is explained by quantization.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using Wien law lambda_max = b/T, Stefan-Boltzmann reasoning P = A sigma T^4, and explaining that Planck quantization resolves the spectrum shape.
answer_move: Start with the temperature change; then decide how peak wavelength and total emitted power change.
common_point_loss: Thinking a hotter blackbody emits only one wavelength instead of a continuous spectrum with a shifted peak.

title: The Photoelectric Effect
what_it_is: Photoelectrons are emitted only when photon energy exceeds the work function, with maximum kinetic energy K_max = hf - phi.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by checking threshold frequency, using K_max = hf - phi, relating stopping potential to K_max, and treating provided work functions as data rather than memorized constants.
answer_move: Check the threshold first; if emission occurs, use photon energy minus work function to find maximum kinetic energy.
common_point_loss: Saying brighter low-frequency light eventually ejects electrons if the intensity is large enough.

title: Compton Scattering
what_it_is: Compton scattering shows a photon colliding with an electron and leaving with lower energy, lower frequency, and longer wavelength.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by conserving energy and momentum, using Delta lambda = h/(m_e c)(1 - cos theta), and describing the scattered photon as longer wavelength after giving energy to the electron.
answer_move: Draw before-and-after momentum vectors; then connect the photon wavelength increase to energy transferred to the electron.
common_point_loss: Treating the photon as slowing down in vacuum rather than changing frequency and wavelength while still traveling at c.

title: Fission, Fusion, and Nuclear Decay
what_it_is: Nuclear reactions and decays conserve charge, nucleon number, energy, and momentum, while mass-energy changes are related by E = mc^2.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by balancing nuclear equations, using conservation laws, relating mass difference to energy, and applying lambda = ln2/t_1/2 or N = N0e^(-lambda t) when decay is modeled quantitatively.
answer_move: Balance nucleon number and charge first; then use mass-energy or exponential decay only after the reaction bookkeeping is consistent.
common_point_loss: Balancing only electric charge and forgetting nucleon number or emitted particles.

title: Types of Radioactive Decay
what_it_is: Alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus, and gamma decay change nuclei in distinct ways while conserving charge, nucleon number, lepton number, energy, and momentum.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the emitted particle, updating mass number and atomic number correctly, and staying inside AP scope: no neutron emission, electron capture, neutrino-type details, or weak-force mechanism explanation.
answer_move: Write the emitted particle symbol first; then balance mass number, atomic number, and lepton number.
common_point_loss: Treating gamma decay as changing the element or mass number instead of lowering nuclear energy only.

title: Electric Charge and Electric Force
what_it_is: Coulomb's law describes the electric force between two point charges: proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, directed along the line connecting them, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges.
how_points_are_earned: You must set up Coulomb's law with correct magnitudes and signs, treat force as a vector (superposing components from multiple charges rather than just adding magnitudes), and correctly identify direction from the geometry.
answer_move: For a system of four or fewer point charges, compute each pairwise Coulomb force as a vector, break into components along a chosen axis system, and sum components separately before combining; do not attempt this direct pairwise method for more than four charges or for continuous distributions -- that requires a field or Gauss's-law approach instead.
common_point_loss: Adding force magnitudes directly instead of resolving each pairwise force into components before summing.

title: Conservation of Electric Charge and Charge Distribution
what_it_is: Total electric charge in an isolated system is conserved, and charge can be spread continuously as a density: linear (charge per length), surface (charge per area), or volume (charge per volume).
how_points_are_earned: You must write the correct integral matching the dimensionality of the charge distribution, and if the density isn't uniform, keep it inside the integral rather than pulling it out as a constant.
answer_move: Before integrating, identify whether the charge lives on a line, surface, or volume, name the matching density type, and write the differential element consistent with that choice -- this sets up correctly every later integral in the unit.
common_point_loss: Using the wrong density type for the dimensionality of the object, such as treating a surface charge as if it were a volume charge.

title: Electric Fields
what_it_is: The electric field is the force per unit charge that would act on a small positive test charge at a point in space -- it exists at every point regardless of whether a charge is actually placed there.
how_points_are_earned: You must state or use the force-per-charge field definition correctly (field is a vector, defined at a point independent of any test charge present), and correctly interpret field line diagrams -- direction from lines, relative magnitude from line density.
answer_move: When asked to describe or sketch a field, treat the field as existing at the point itself, independent of any test charge, and use field-line density (not just direction) to communicate relative field strength.
common_point_loss: Describing the field as if it only exists when a test charge is physically present at that point, rather than as a property of space itself.

title: Electric Fields of Charge Distributions
what_it_is: Using calculus to find the electric field produced by a continuous (non-point) charge distribution, by integrating the contributions of infinitesimal charge elements across the distribution.
how_points_are_earned: You must set up the charge element correctly in terms of the relevant density and geometry, express the distance and direction terms as functions of the integration variable, and carry out a definite integral with correct limits.
answer_move: Only attempt direct calculus integration for one of the five specified geometries -- an infinite charged wire/cylinder at a distance from its axis, a ring of charge on its axis, a semicircular arc at its center, or a finite line charge collinear with it or on its perpendicular bisector; for any other shape, this integral is not the intended tool.
common_point_loss: Trying to integrate a full field vector when symmetry cancels one component, instead of first identifying which component survives and integrating only that one.

title: Electric Flux
what_it_is: Electric flux measures how much electric field passes through a surface: the field times the area for a uniform field through a flat surface, or a general surface integral when the field or surface isn't uniform or flat.
how_points_are_earned: You must account for the angle between the field and the surface's area vector (normal direction), recognizing that flux is maximized when the field is parallel to the normal and zero when the field is parallel to the surface itself.
answer_move: Identify the direction of the area vector (outward normal) for the surface in question, then use the field component along that normal direction (or the full integral for non-uniform cases) rather than just multiplying field by area without accounting for orientation.
common_point_loss: Computing flux as field times area without checking whether the field is actually perpendicular to the surface.

title: Gauss's Law
what_it_is: Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by the permittivity of free space.
how_points_are_earned: You must choose a Gaussian surface matching the actual symmetry of the charge (sphere, cylinder, or plane), use the correct area formula for that surface, express the enclosed charge using the fixed dimensions of the actual charged object (not the variable Gaussian-surface radius), and solve for the field.
answer_move: Only use Gauss's law quantitatively when the charge distribution has spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry; for a cylindrical setup specifically, use the curved lateral surface area (never a disk's or sphere's area formula), and compute enclosed charge from the charged object's own fixed radius, not the Gaussian surface's radius.
common_point_loss: For a cylindrical Gaussian surface, using a sphere's or disk's area formula instead of the cylinder's lateral area, or plugging the Gaussian surface's own radius into the enclosed-charge calculation instead of the charged object's actual radius.

title: Electric Potential Energy
what_it_is: Electric potential energy is the energy stored in a charge configuration. For two point charges, U = k q1 q2 / r, with the sign coming from the charge signs and the distance measured between the charges.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using the signs of both charges, the separation between charges, and superposition when more than one interacting pair contributes to the system energy.
answer_move: Before calculating U, list the interacting charge pairs and write the sign of q1 q2 for each pair; then add pair energies as scalars, not as force vectors.
common_point_loss: Dropping the sign of q1 q2 and reporting every electric potential energy as positive.

title: Electric Potential
what_it_is: Electric potential is electric potential energy per unit charge. For point charges, V = kq/r, and potentials from multiple charges add as scalars even when the electric fields from those charges must be added as vectors.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by adding potentials with signs but no directions, using deltaV = - integral E dot dr when deriving potential difference from a field, and restricting calculus-based potential derivations to the approved geometries.
answer_move: First decide whether the prompt asks for field or potential: field needs vector components, but potential needs signed scalar terms added directly.
common_point_loss: Canceling electric potential because equal and opposite field components cancel at the point.

title: Conservation of Electric Energy
what_it_is: Conservation of electric energy tracks how electric potential energy changes into kinetic energy or other energy stores. The key relationship is deltaU = q deltaV, combined with total mechanical/electric energy conservation when nonconservative work is absent.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by computing deltaU = q deltaV with the sign of q included, then applying energy conservation consistently instead of assuming every move to lower potential increases kinetic energy for every charge sign.
answer_move: Write deltaU = q(V_f - V_i) before judging speed changes; the sign of the moving charge decides whether a given potential change raises or lowers electric potential energy.
common_point_loss: Saying lower electric potential always means lower electric potential energy, even for a negative charge.

what_it_is: Electrostatics with Conductors is the Conductors and Capacitors topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: use conductor electrostatic-equilibrium facts: zero internal field, equipotential conductor, perpendicular surface field, and surface charge.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you use conductor electrostatic-equilibrium facts: zero internal field, equipotential conductor, perpendicular surface field, and surface charge, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then use conductor electrostatic-equilibrium facts: zero internal field, equipotential conductor, perpendicular surface field, and surface charge before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Putting excess charge throughout the conductor's volume instead of on its surface

title: Redistribution of Charge Between Conductors
what_it_is: Redistribution of Charge Between Conductors is the Conductors and Capacitors topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: apply charge conservation and equal final potential when connected conductors share charge.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you apply charge conservation and equal final potential when connected conductors share charge, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then apply charge conservation and equal final potential when connected conductors share charge before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Assuming identical final charges when the conductors have different capacitances or radii

title: Capacitors
what_it_is: Capacitors is the Conductors and Capacitors topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: derive capacitance from C equals Q over Delta V for the allowed geometry instead of defaulting to parallel plates.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you derive capacitance from C equals Q over Delta V for the allowed geometry instead of defaulting to parallel plates, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then derive capacitance from C equals Q over Delta V for the allowed geometry instead of defaulting to parallel plates before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Force-fitting a cylindrical or spherical capacitor into C equals kappa epsilon0 A over d

title: Dielectrics
what_it_is: Dielectrics is the Conductors and Capacitors topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: explain dielectric polarization and use kappa relationships for field reduction, capacitance increase, and stored energy changes.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you explain dielectric polarization and use kappa relationships for field reduction, capacitance increase, and stored energy changes, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then explain dielectric polarization and use kappa relationships for field reduction, capacitance increase, and stored energy changes before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Treating a dielectric as if it adds free charge to the capacitor plates

title: Magnetic Fields
what_it_is: Magnetic fields are vector fields with no isolated magnetic monopoles. Gauss's law for magnetism states that net magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by representing magnetic-field direction, using closed-loop field-line reasoning, and explaining why a closed surface has zero net magnetic flux.
answer_move: Start with the field map: magnetic field lines loop, so any flux entering a closed surface must also leave it.
common_point_loss: Treating a magnetic north pole like an isolated electric charge source with field lines beginning there and ending nowhere.

title: Magnetism and Moving Charges
what_it_is: A moving charge in a magnetic field experiences force F_B = q(v x B). The force is perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field and reverses for negative charge.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by applying the right-hand rule with charge sign, using the vector cross product or qvB sin(theta), and not confusing point-charge force with wire-force formulas.
answer_move: Use v cross B for a positive charge, then reverse the result if q is negative; only after direction is set should you compute magnitude.
common_point_loss: Using the current-carrying-wire force integral for a moving point charge.

title: Magnetic Fields of Current-Carrying Wires and the Biot-Savart Law
what_it_is: The Biot-Savart law builds magnetic field from current elements: dB is proportional to I dl x rhat over r^2. Quantitative AP use is limited to specified symmetric conductor geometries.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining dl and rhat, using the cross product direction, respecting the allowed geometries, and integrating or citing derived results only when symmetry permits.
answer_move: Draw the current element and point of interest, mark rhat from the element to the point, then apply dl x rhat before setting up the integral.
common_point_loss: Using B = mu0 I/(2 pi r) for every current geometry instead of checking whether the long-straight-wire symmetry applies.

title: Ampere's Law
what_it_is: Ampere's law relates circulation of magnetic field around a closed loop to enclosed current: integral B dot dl = mu0 I_enc. It is powerful when symmetry makes B constant on the loop.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing an Amperian loop that matches symmetry, evaluating B dot dl along the loop, and calculating enclosed current correctly, including from current density when needed.
answer_move: Pick the loop after identifying symmetry; then compute I_enc for the current actually passing through the loop surface before solving for B.
common_point_loss: Substituting total current when only part of a distributed current is enclosed by the Amperian loop.

title: Scalars and Vectors
what_it_is: A scalar is a quantity fully described by a magnitude alone (like speed or distance), while a vector requires both magnitude and direction (like velocity or displacement). In this course vectors are written in unit vector notation and combined by adding or subtracting their components separately.
how_points_are_earned: Points come from correctly resolving a given vector into its component directions, then adding or subtracting component-by-component to find a resultant -- not from stating a final magnitude without showing the component work.
answer_move: When asked for a resultant vector, add or subtract the components in each direction separately before recombining, and keep each component's sign tied to its assigned axis direction throughout.
common_point_loss: Combining vector magnitudes directly (like adding lengths) instead of adding matching components separately.

title: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration
what_it_is: Displacement, average velocity, and average acceleration describe motion over a finite time interval, but instantaneous velocity and acceleration are true derivatives of position and velocity with respect to time. This is the calculus-based definition -- position, velocity, and acceleration are treated as functions of time that can be differentiated or integrated into one another.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned by correctly differentiating a given position or velocity function (or integrating in the reverse direction), and by clearly identifying whether a question is asking for an average quantity versus an instantaneous one -- these are graded as distinct calculations.
answer_move: When a position or velocity function is given as an explicit expression in time, differentiate it directly to get instantaneous velocity or acceleration -- do not fall back on average-rate formulas, which only apply when you're working from two data points, not a continuous function.
common_point_loss: Using the average velocity or average acceleration formula when the question actually asks for an instantaneous value at a specific time.

title: Representing Motion
what_it_is: Under constant acceleration, motion is described by the familiar kinematic equations. When acceleration or velocity is not constant, position and velocity changes are instead found by integrating velocity or acceleration over the given time interval.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned by first identifying whether acceleration is constant (justifying use of the kinematic equations) or a function of time (requiring integration), then executing the correct algebra or integral with correct limits of integration.
answer_move: Before choosing a method, check whether acceleration is stated or shown to be constant; if it is not constant, set up the correct integral with the correct time bounds instead of reaching for the constant-acceleration equations, which do not apply.
common_point_loss: Applying the constant-acceleration kinematic equations to a situation where acceleration is explicitly given as a function of time.

title: Reference Frames and Relative Motion
what_it_is: The reference frame you choose determines the magnitude and direction you measure for a moving object's velocity; converting a measurement from one inertial frame to another is done by vector addition or subtraction. Acceleration, however, is the same in every inertial frame. Unlike the algebra-based course, relative-velocity vector addition here is not restricted to one dimension -- full two-dimensional relative-velocity scenarios are in scope.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned by correctly setting up a vector equation relating the object's velocity in one frame to its velocity in another and resolving it by components when the motion is two-dimensional, not by combining speeds as scalars.
answer_move: For a relative-velocity problem, write the vector equation linking the two frames component-by-component (including both dimensions when the scenario is 2D, such as a boat-and-current problem) rather than adding or subtracting speeds directly.
common_point_loss: Adding relative velocities as plain numbers instead of as vectors, which drops the perpendicular component of motion entirely.

title: Motion in Two or Three Dimensions
what_it_is: Motion in two dimensions is analyzed by splitting it into independent one-dimensional components along each axis -- each axis can have its own velocity and acceleration, and a change in motion along one axis does not affect the other. This course's quantitative ceiling is two dimensions; three-dimensional motion is only expected to be described qualitatively, not calculated.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned by explicitly separating the motion into components along each axis, applying the correct kinematic or integral relationship independently to each axis, and only recombining components at the end.
answer_move: Set up separate equations for each axis using that axis's own acceleration and initial velocity before solving, and only combine the two results at the very last step when a single resultant quantity (like speed or range) is requested.
common_point_loss: Letting the acceleration or time used in one direction's equation leak into the other direction's calculation instead of keeping the two axes fully separate.

title: Systems and Center of Mass
what_it_is: A system is the chosen collection of objects. Center of mass locates the system average position, using sums for particles or integrals for continuous mass distributions.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by defining the system, writing the correct mass-weighted sum or integral, choosing density and limits, and using center-of-mass motion for external-force analysis.
answer_move: Draw the system boundary first; then choose a particle sum or r_cm = integral r dm over integral dm based on whether the mass is discrete or continuous.
common_point_loss: Using a geometric midpoint as center of mass without checking the mass distribution.

title: Forces and Free-Body Diagrams
what_it_is: Forces are vector interactions exerted on an object or system. A free-body diagram shows individual force arrows from the center-of-mass dot, not components.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing only forces exerted on the selected object, labeling interaction partners when useful, keeping same-direction forces side by side, and choosing helpful axes.
answer_move: Choose the object, then draw one arrow for each external force on it before resolving components in equations.
common_point_loss: Drawing component arrows on the FBD as if they were additional forces.

title: Newton's Third Law
what_it_is: Newton's third law pairs are equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces exerted on different objects. Internal third-law pairs do not change system center-of-mass motion.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying which object each force acts on, excluding internal forces from a system net-force sum, and not assuming massive-string tension is uniform.
answer_move: Name both objects in the interaction pair: force by A on B and force by B on A. Then decide whether each force is internal or external to the chosen system.
common_point_loss: Putting both third-law forces on the same free-body diagram for one object.

title: Newton's First Law
what_it_is: Newton's first law says velocity is constant in an inertial frame when net force is zero. Balanced forces can apply in one direction while another direction accelerates.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by setting the vector net force to zero only for directions in equilibrium and by stating when an observer frame can be treated as inertial.
answer_move: Check each axis separately: if acceleration is zero along that axis, write sum F for that axis equals zero.
common_point_loss: Assuming an object moving at constant speed in one direction has zero net force in every direction.

title: Newton's Second Law
what_it_is: Newton's second law connects net external force to center-of-mass acceleration: a_sys = F_net/m_sys for constant-mass systems.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by summing external forces on the selected system, writing component equations, matching acceleration directions, and using mass of the system represented by the equation.
answer_move: After the FBD, write sum F_x = m a_x and sum F_y = m a_y for the same object or system; keep constraints on separate lines.
common_point_loss: Mixing forces from different objects into one equation without defining a system.

title: Gravitational Force
what_it_is: Gravitational force is attractive and follows F_g = Gm1m2/r^2 along the line between centers of mass. Gravitational field is g = GM/r^2.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing the interacting masses and separation, distinguishing weight from normal force, and applying shell-theorem results only for spherical mass distributions.
answer_move: Identify whether the question asks for force, field, weight, or apparent weight; then choose mg, GMm/r^2, or a shell-theorem result accordingly.
common_point_loss: Treating apparent weight as always equal to gravitational force even when the object accelerates.

title: Kinetic and Static Friction
what_it_is: Kinetic friction has magnitude mu_k F_N and opposes sliding. Static friction adjusts up to a maximum: F_s <= mu_s F_N, reaching equality only at impending slip.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by deciding whether the contact is sliding or not, using kinetic friction as an equality, using static friction as an inequality, and finding its direction from relative motion tendency.
answer_move: Ask whether the surfaces slide. If not, solve for the static friction needed first, then compare it to mu_s F_N only as a limit.
common_point_loss: Setting F_s = mu_s F_N in every static-friction problem.

title: Spring Forces
what_it_is: An ideal spring exerts F_s = -k Delta x toward equilibrium. Equivalent spring constants can be found for purely series or purely parallel spring systems.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying displacement from equilibrium, assigning the restoring-force direction, and using series or parallel formulas only for those allowed arrangements.
answer_move: Draw how the springs share force or displacement; then choose k_parallel = sum k_i or 1/k_series = sum 1/k_i.
common_point_loss: Treating parallel springs as if their equivalent constant follows the series reciprocal rule.

title: Resistive Forces
what_it_is: Resistive forces depend on velocity and oppose motion, such as F_r = -kv. Newton's second law becomes a differential equation for velocity.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by writing the net-force differential equation, separating variables with correct limits, solving for v(t) or a related quantity, and identifying terminal velocity from net force zero.
answer_move: Start with sum F = m dv/dt including the velocity-dependent force; then separate variables instead of using constant-acceleration kinematics.
common_point_loss: Using constant-acceleration equations when the net force depends on velocity.

title: Circular Motion
what_it_is: Circular motion has centripetal acceleration v^2/r toward the center plus any tangential acceleration when speed changes. Forces or force components supply the inward net force.
how_points_are_earned: You earn points by drawing the FBD, resolving radial and tangential components, setting sum F_radial = mv^2/r, and using period/orbit relations only under their assumptions.
answer_move: Choose inward as the radial positive direction, then write the radial net-force equation separately from any tangential equation.
common_point_loss: Calling centripetal force a new force instead of the inward net force from real interactions.

title: Translational Kinetic Energy
what_it_is: Translational Kinetic Energy is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: compute kinetic energy as a scalar and keep reference-frame dependence in mind.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you compute kinetic energy as a scalar and keep reference-frame dependence in mind, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then compute kinetic energy as a scalar and keep reference-frame dependence in mind before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Assigning a sign to kinetic energy because velocity has a sign

title: Work
what_it_is: Work is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: set up work as a dot product or line integral and reduce to F parallel times displacement when force is constant.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you set up work as a dot product or line integral and reduce to F parallel times displacement when force is constant, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then set up work as a dot product or line integral and reduce to F parallel times displacement when force is constant before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Using constant-force work formulas for a variable force without integrating or using graph area

title: Potential Energy
what_it_is: Potential Energy is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: connect conservative-force work to changes in potential energy and use slope or derivative relationships when appropriate.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you connect conservative-force work to changes in potential energy and use slope or derivative relationships when appropriate, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then connect conservative-force work to changes in potential energy and use slope or derivative relationships when appropriate before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Treating spring potential energy as negative when a spring is compressed

title: Conservation of Energy
what_it_is: Conservation of Energy is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: identify all energy terms in initial and final states before substituting into a conservation equation.
how_points_are_earned: Points are earned when you identify all energy terms in initial and final states before substituting into a conservation equation, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
answer_move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then identify all energy terms in initial and final states before substituting into a conservation equation before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.
common_point_loss: Omitting one spring, gravitational, or kinetic term from the selected system's energy equation

title: Power
what_it_is: Power is the Work, Energy, and Power topic where you turn the concept into an AP-ready action: use average power as energy per time and instantaneous power as dW/dt or force dot velocity.
